title: The Columbian Exchange
subtitle: The transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the hemispheres after 1492
summary: The “Columbian Exchange,” a term coined by the historian Alfred W. Crosby, describes the enormous transfer of crops, livestock, people, and microbes between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres that followed 1492. Maize and potatoes transformed diets in Europe, Africa, and Asia; horses, cattle, and wheat transformed the Americas. Most devastating of all, Old World diseases such as smallpox and measles killed a large share of the Native peoples of the Americas.
thumbAlt: Illustration from the Florentine Codex showing Nahua people suffering from smallpox

title: The Digital Revolution
subtitle: Computers, the internet, and smartphones transform American life
summary: The digital revolution is the transformation of the economy and daily life by computers and networked communication. Its roots lie in government-funded research: the Defense Department’s ARPANET began with four computers in 1969, and the National Science Foundation’s NSFNET, launched in 1986, became the backbone of the early internet. In the 1990s personal computers and the web turned the internet into a mass phenomenon and fueled the dot-com boom; after 2007, smartphones and social media put the internet in Americans’ pockets.
thumbAlt: Logical map of the ARPANET in September 1973

title: Federalism
subtitle: How power is divided between the national government and the states
summary: Federalism is the division of governing power between a national government and the states. The Constitution gives the federal government specific powers, makes federal law supreme within its sphere, and leaves the rest to the states and the people. Where to draw that line, over slavery, commerce, civil rights, and social welfare, has been one of the most persistent arguments in American history.

title: Jazz
subtitle: America’s homegrown music, born in New Orleans
summary: Jazz is an American musical style built on improvisation and syncopated rhythm. It grew out of New Orleans around 1900, where African, Caribbean, Creole, and European traditions, brass bands, ragtime, and the blues met. Popularized by the city’s African American community and spread by records and radio, it became a national sensation in the 1920s, the decade often called the Jazz Age, and then a music heard around the world.
thumbAlt: Promotional card of the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, which made the first commercial jazz recording in 1917

title: Jim Crow
subtitle: The system of legal segregation and disenfranchisement, 1880s–1960s
summary: “Jim Crow” was the system of laws and customs that segregated Black Americans and stripped them of the vote after Reconstruction, named after a Black character in minstrel shows. From the 1880s into the 1960s, Southern states, and many others, required separate schools, railroad cars, waiting rooms, and cemeteries, and they barred Black men from voting with poll taxes and literacy tests. The Supreme Court approved “separate but equal” facilities in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896, and the whole system was enforced by violence, including thousands of lynchings. The civil rights movement, Brown v. Board of Education, and the civil rights laws of 1964 and 1965 finally dismantled it.
thumbAlt: A segregation sign in Durham, North Carolina

title: Manifest Destiny
subtitle: The belief that the United States was destined to spread across the continent
summary: “Manifest Destiny” was the phrase, first used by the editor John O’Sullivan in 1845, for the belief that the United States had a God-given right and duty to expand across North America. It gave a name to an outlook that justified the annexation of Texas, the acquisition of Oregon, and the war with Mexico, and that treated Native nations and Mexicans as obstacles to American progress.
thumbAlt: John Gast’s painting American Progress, showing a floating female figure leading settlers westward

title: Republicanism
subtitle: The founders’ ideal of self-government by virtuous citizens
summary: In the American founding era, republicanism meant government without a king, resting on the people and run by their elected representatives, but it also meant a set of fears and hopes about liberty. Republicans worried that power corrupts, that luxury and dependence destroy virtue, and that free governments survive only if citizens put the public good ahead of private interest. These ideas shaped the Revolution, the Constitution, and early American politics.

title: Slavery in America
subtitle: The institution that shaped the nation’s economy, politics, and conflicts for nearly 250 years
summary: Slavery, the ownership of human beings as property, inherited by their children and enforced by law and violence, was legal in every one of the thirteen colonies and lasted in the United States until 1865. Enslaved Africans and their descendants grew the tobacco, rice, and above all the cotton that made the South rich and drove the nation’s exports. By 1860 the census counted 3,953,760 enslaved people, about one in eight Americans. The struggle over slavery shaped the Constitution, split the nation in the 1850s, and ended only with the Civil War and the Thirteenth Amendment.
thumbAlt: Wilson Chinn, a formerly enslaved man from Louisiana, photographed in 1863

title: The Blues
subtitle: The African American music of the Deep South that became the root of jazz, rock and roll, and soul
summary: The blues is a music created by African Americans in the Deep South around the 1880s and 1890s, at about the same time as jazz and ragtime. Built on a twelve-bar pattern of chords and the bent “blue notes” that give it its sound, it grew from work songs, field hollers, and spirituals, and it spoke of hard labor, poverty, love, and life under Jim Crow. The Mississippi Delta, often called its birthplace, produced many of its greatest performers. Carried north by the Great Migration and electrified in Chicago, the blues became a foundation for much of American popular music.
thumbAlt: Portrait of the composer and bandleader W. C. Handy in 1941

title: The Gilded Age
subtitle: An era of industrial wealth, inequality, and corruption, c. 1870–1900
summary: “The Gilded Age” names the decades after Reconstruction, when the United States became the world’s leading industrial economy. The term comes from an 1873 satirical novel by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner, and it describes a glittering surface of wealth and innovation covering deep inequality and corruption. Railroads, steel, oil, and finance created vast fortunes, while millions of workers and immigrants crowded into cities and fought for decent wages and conditions.
thumbAlt: Joseph Keppler’s cartoon of giant moneybags representing trusts looming over the U.S. Senate

title: Brown v. Board of Education
subtitle: The Supreme Court strikes down school segregation
summary: In Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, decided May 17, 1954, a unanimous Supreme Court held that racial segregation in public schools violates the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of equal protection of the laws. “Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal,” Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote, overturning the “separate but equal” doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson in public education. The victory crowned decades of NAACP litigation led by Thurgood Marshall. But the Court’s vague order to desegregate “with all deliberate speed” met fierce resistance, and most Southern schools were not integrated until the late 1960s and early 1970s.
thumbAlt: The Supreme Court’s judgment in Brown v. Board of Education

title: Dred Scott v. Sandford
subtitle: The Supreme Court denies Black citizenship and opens the territories to slavery, 1857
summary: Dred Scott, an enslaved man, and his wife, Harriet, sued for their freedom in 1846 because their enslaver had held them for years at army posts in free territory. After an eleven-year legal struggle, the Supreme Court ruled against them on March 6, 1857. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney declared that people of African descent could not be citizens of the United States, and that Congress had no power to ban slavery from the federal territories, which meant the Missouri Compromise had been unconstitutional. Meant to settle the slavery question, the decision inflamed it and moved the nation closer to civil war. The National Archives notes that many legal scholars consider it the worst decision the Court has ever issued. The Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments overturned it.
thumbAlt: The Supreme Court’s judgment in Dred Scott v. Sandford

title: Korematsu v. United States
subtitle: The Supreme Court upholds the wartime exclusion of Japanese Americans
summary: Fred Korematsu, a 23-year-old American citizen of Japanese ancestry, refused to leave his home in the San Francisco Bay Area when the Army ordered all Japanese Americans removed under Executive Order 9066. In Korematsu v. United States, the Supreme Court upheld his conviction 6–3, accepting the government’s claim of military necessity. Three justices dissented, one of them condemning the decision as racism. Decades later, evidence that the government had suppressed proof undermining its case led a federal court to overturn Korematsu’s conviction.
thumbAlt: Fred Korematsu

title: Loving v. Virginia
subtitle: The Supreme Court strikes down bans on interracial marriage
summary: Mildred Jeter, a Black woman, and Richard Loving, a white man, married in Washington, D.C., in 1958 and returned home to Virginia, where they were convicted of violating the state’s ban on interracial marriage. In Loving v. Virginia (1967), a unanimous Supreme Court struck down the law, holding that it violated both the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. “The freedom to marry, or not marry, a person of another race resides with the individual,” Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote, “and cannot be infringed by the State.”
thumbAlt: Mildred and Richard Loving

title: Marbury v. Madison
subtitle: The case in which the Supreme Court first struck down an act of Congress
summary: In Marbury v. Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall turned a minor dispute over an undelivered job commission into the foundation of American judicial power. The Court ruled that William Marbury was entitled to his commission but that it could not order it delivered, because the law giving the Court that power was itself unconstitutional. In declaring an act of Congress void, the Court claimed the power of judicial review, the authority to decide whether laws conform to the Constitution.
thumbAlt: First page of the Supreme Court’s opinion in Marbury v. Madison

title: McCulloch v. Maryland
subtitle: The Supreme Court upholds broad federal power and bars states from taxing the national bank
summary: When Maryland taxed the Baltimore branch of the Second Bank of the United States, the bank’s cashier, James McCulloch, refused to pay. In 1819 the Supreme Court, speaking through Chief Justice John Marshall, ruled that Congress had the implied power to charter a bank under the Constitution’s “necessary and proper” clause, and that states could not tax the federal government, because “the power to tax involves the power to destroy.” The decision became a cornerstone of national power.
thumbAlt: Page from the Supreme Court’s decision in McCulloch v. Maryland

title: Miranda v. Arizona
subtitle: The ruling that requires police to warn suspects of their rights
summary: In Miranda v. Arizona (1966), the Supreme Court held that the Fifth Amendment’s protection against self-incrimination applies to police interrogation. Before questioning a suspect in custody, police must warn that the suspect has the right to remain silent, that anything said can be used in court, and that the suspect has the right to a lawyer, appointed if necessary. These requirements became known as “Miranda warnings.”
thumbAlt: Document from Miranda v. Arizona signed by Chief Justice Earl Warren

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
subtitle: The Supreme Court upholds “separate but equal,” 1896
summary: In 1892 Homer Plessy, a New Orleans man who was seven-eighths white, deliberately sat in a whites-only railroad car to challenge Louisiana’s law requiring segregated trains. On May 18, 1896, the Supreme Court upheld the law by 7 to 1, ruling that “equal but separate” accommodations did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment. Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented alone, declaring that “our constitution is color-blind.” The decision gave constitutional approval to the Jim Crow system of segregation for more than half a century, until Brown v. Board of Education rejected it in 1954.
thumbAlt: The Supreme Court’s judgment in Plessy v. Ferguson

title: Roe v. Wade
subtitle: The 1973 decision recognizing a constitutional right to abortion, overruled in 2022
summary: In Roe v. Wade (1973), the Supreme Court held 7–2 that the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause protects a “right to privacy” broad enough to include a woman’s decision whether to have an abortion. The Court struck down a Texas law that banned abortion except to save the woman’s life and set out a framework based on the trimesters of pregnancy. Roe became one of the most contested decisions in American history. In 2022, in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the Court overruled it, holding that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion.
thumbAlt: Official 1976 portrait of Justice Harry A. Blackmun, author of the majority opinion in Roe v. Wade

title: Schenck v. United States
subtitle: Free speech in wartime and the “clear and present danger” test, 1919
summary: During World War I, socialists Charles Schenck and Elizabeth Baer mailed leaflets urging men to resist the draft, which they called involuntary servitude. Convicted under the Espionage Act, they argued that the law violated the First Amendment. In 1919 a unanimous Supreme Court upheld their convictions. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes introduced the “clear and present danger” test and compared their leaflets to falsely shouting “fire” in a crowded theater.
thumbAlt: The antidraft leaflet distributed by Charles Schenck

title: United States v. Nixon
subtitle: The Supreme Court orders the president to release the Watergate tapes
summary: In United States v. Nixon, decided July 24, 1974, the Supreme Court unanimously rejected President Richard Nixon’s claim that “executive privilege” allowed him to withhold White House tape recordings subpoenaed in the Watergate prosecutions. The Court recognized a limited privilege but held that it must yield to the needs of the criminal justice system. The tapes Nixon was forced to release led to his resignation sixteen days later.
thumbAlt: The edited transcripts of the White House tapes released by Nixon

title: Worcester v. Georgia
subtitle: The Supreme Court recognizes Cherokee sovereignty, and the president refuses to enforce it
summary: Samuel Worcester, a missionary living in the Cherokee Nation, was imprisoned by Georgia for refusing to obtain a state license. In 1832 the Supreme Court ruled that the Cherokee Nation was “a distinct community occupying its own territory in which the laws of Georgia can have no force,” and that only the federal government could deal with it. The decision affirmed tribal sovereignty in principle, but Georgia ignored it and President Jackson declined to enforce it, and the Cherokee were forcibly removed six years later.
thumbAlt: First issue of the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper, printed in English and Cherokee

title: Articles of Confederation
subtitle: The first constitution of the United States, 1781–1789
summary: The Articles of Confederation created the first government of the United States: a “league of friendship” among thirteen sovereign states, with a one-house Congress in which each state had a single vote. Written during the Revolution by men wary of distant central power, the Articles gave Congress little ability to tax, regulate trade, or enforce its decisions. Their weaknesses led directly to the Constitutional Convention of 1787.
thumbAlt: First page of the Articles of Confederation

title: The Bill of Rights
subtitle: The first ten amendments to the Constitution
summary: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution, ratified on December 15, 1791. It protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, and assembly, the right to bear arms, security against unreasonable searches, and the rights of people accused of crimes, and it reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people. It was added to answer Anti-Federalist critics who feared that the new national government would trample individual liberties. James Madison, once its opponent, guided it through the First Congress. At first it limited only the federal government. The author of the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) meant that amendment to make the Bill of Rights binding on the states as well, a question the Supreme Court long resisted.
thumbAlt: The engrossed Bill of Rights as sent to the states in 1789

title: The Chinese Exclusion Act
subtitle: The first federal law to bar immigrants by nationality, 1882
summary: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred Chinese laborers from immigrating to the United States for ten years, the first time federal law excluded people on the basis of nationality and race. Extended and tightened in 1892 and made permanent in 1902, exclusion lasted until 1943. It shaped Chinese American life for generations and set the pattern for later laws restricting immigration from Asia and other parts of the world.
thumbAlt: Page of the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882

title: Civil Rights Act of 1964
subtitle: The law that outlawed segregation in public places and job discrimination
summary: The Civil Rights Act of 1964, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson on July 2, 1964, outlawed segregation in hotels, restaurants, theaters, and other public accommodations. It banned discrimination in employment, authorized federal action to desegregate schools and public facilities, and created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. The National Archives calls it “the most sweeping civil rights legislation since Reconstruction.” Proposed by John F. Kennedy after the protests of 1963, it was pushed through Congress after his assassination by Johnson and a bipartisan coalition, overcoming a Southern filibuster of 75 days. Together with the Voting Rights Act a year later, the American Yawp concludes, it “effectively ended Jim Crow.”
thumbAlt: President Lyndon Johnson signing the Civil Rights Act of 1964, surrounded by onlookers

title: The Constitution of the United States
subtitle: The framework of the federal government, written in 1787 and amended twenty-seven times
summary: The Constitution, drafted in secret at a convention in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787 and signed on September 17, replaced the weak Articles of Confederation with a strong national government of three branches, each able to check the others. It was a document of compromises: between large and small states, between North and South, and between those who wanted a powerful central government and those who feared one. Ratified in 1788 after a fierce public debate, and soon amended by the Bill of Rights, it has governed the United States ever since.
thumbAlt: The first page of the original engrossed Constitution, beginning “We the People”

title: The Dawes Act
subtitle: Breaking up tribal lands through allotment, 1887
summary: The Dawes Act, or General Allotment Act, authorized the president to break up reservation land held in common by Native nations and divide it into individual allotments, 160 acres to each head of family, smaller parcels to others. Its sponsors presented it as a humanitarian reform that would turn Native people into independent farmers and assimilate them into white American society. In practice it undermined tribal sovereignty, opened “surplus” land to white settlement, and contributed to a massive loss of Native land.
thumbAlt: First page of the Dawes Act

title: The Declaration of Independence
subtitle: The Continental Congress explains why thirteen colonies are breaking with Britain
summary: The Declaration of Independence, adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, announced that the thirteen American colonies were “Free and Independent States” and explained to the world why they were breaking with Great Britain. Drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson, it is best remembered for its preamble: “We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal,” with rights to “Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.” The men who adopted it did not mean it to end slavery or give everyone political rights. Yet, as the American Yawp observes, most of the conflicts of American history since then have been struggles over what it means to believe that “all men are created equal.”
thumbAlt: John Trumbull’s painting of the Committee of Five presenting the draft Declaration of Independence to the Continental Congress

title: The Emancipation Proclamation
subtitle: Lincoln declares freedom for enslaved people in the Confederacy, 1863
summary: On January 1, 1863, President Abraham Lincoln declared that “all persons held as slaves” in the areas then in rebellion against the United States “are, and henceforward shall be free.” He issued it as commander in chief, calling it “a fit and necessary war measure.” It did not apply to the loyal border states or to parts of the Confederacy already under Union control, and it depended on Union victory to take effect. Even so, it changed the character of the Civil War. Every advance of Union troops now widened the territory of freedom, and the proclamation opened the Army and Navy to Black men, almost 200,000 of whom served.
thumbAlt: Francis Bicknell Carpenter’s painting of Lincoln reading the Emancipation Proclamation to his cabinet

title: Executive Order 9066
subtitle: The 1942 order that led to the incarceration of Japanese Americans
summary: Signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on February 19, 1942, ten weeks after Pearl Harbor, Executive Order 9066 authorized the Secretary of War and military commanders to designate “military areas” and exclude anyone from them. The order named no ethnic group, but it was used to remove about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast, most of them U.S. citizens, and confine them in camps for the rest of the war.
thumbAlt: Exclusion orders posted on a brick wall at First and Front Streets, San Francisco, April 1942, directing the removal of people of Japanese ancestry

title: The Federalist Papers
subtitle: Eighty-five essays defending the proposed Constitution
summary: The Federalist is a series of 85 essays written in 1787–88 by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay, under the shared pen name “Publius,” to persuade New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution. Written fast and for a newspaper audience, the essays became the most influential explanation of how the Constitution was meant to work, and courts still cite them today.
thumbAlt: Title page of the first edition of The Federalist

title: The Fifteenth Amendment
subtitle: Barring racial discrimination in voting, 1870
summary: The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified on February 3, 1870, declares that the right of citizens to vote “shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” The last of the three Reconstruction amendments, it gave Black men the vote nationwide, and within weeks the first Black member of Congress took his seat. Because it did not bar discrimination by sex, it split the movement for women’s suffrage. After Reconstruction, Southern states used literacy tests, grandfather clauses, other legal devices, and violence to get around it. Its promise was not enforced until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
thumbAlt: Lithograph celebrating the Fifteenth Amendment

title: The Fourteenth Amendment
subtitle: Citizenship, due process, and equal protection of the laws, 1868
summary: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, made “all persons born or naturalized in the United States” citizens. It forbade any state to deprive any person of “life, liberty, or property, without due process of law” or to deny anyone “the equal protection of the laws.” Written by the Republican Congress during Reconstruction, it granted citizenship to formerly enslaved people and was meant to secure their rights. For decades courts read it narrowly, and in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) the Supreme Court upheld segregation. Its equal protection clause later became the basis of Brown v. Board of Education (1954) and much of modern civil rights law.
thumbAlt: First page of the Fourteenth Amendment

title: The Gettysburg Address
subtitle: Lincoln’s brief speech on the meaning of the war
summary: On November 19, 1863, at the dedication of the Soldiers’ National Cemetery at Gettysburg, President Abraham Lincoln spoke for about two minutes, after the orator Edward Everett had spoken for two hours. Reaching back to 1776 with the words “Four score and seven years ago,” he described the Civil War as a test of whether a nation “dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal” could endure. He called on the living to finish the soldiers’ “unfinished work,” so that the nation would have “a new birth of freedom” and “government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.” It became one of the most celebrated speeches in American history.
thumbAlt: Lincoln’s handwritten Bliss copy of the Gettysburg Address

title: G.I. Bill
subtitle: The Servicemen’s Readjustment Act of 1944
summary: The Servicemen’s Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the G.I. Bill, gave World War II veterans money for college or job training, low-cost home loans, and unemployment pay. About 2.3 million veterans attended college under it, and millions more received vocational or on-the-job training; by 1955 it had backed 4.3 million home loans. The law helped build the postwar middle class, though discrimination kept many Black veterans from sharing fully in its benefits.
thumbAlt: President Franklin D. Roosevelt signing the G.I. Bill

title: Homestead Act
subtitle: The 1862 law that offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and farmed it for five years
summary: Signed by President Abraham Lincoln on May 20, 1862, in the middle of the Civil War, the Homestead Act offered 160 acres of surveyed public land to any adult citizen, or immigrant who intended to become one, who had never taken up arms against the United States. Settlers paid a small filing fee, lived on the land, and farmed it; after five years it was theirs. More than 270 million acres, about a tenth of the nation’s land, passed to private owners under the law, which drew millions of Americans and immigrants onto the Great Plains, land that was already home to American Indian nations.
thumbAlt: A homesteading family posed with their horses and cow in front of their sod house in Custer County, Nebraska

title: Immigration Act of 1924
subtitle: The Johnson-Reed Act and the national origins quota system
summary: The Immigration Act of 1924, also called the Johnson-Reed Act, sharply limited immigration through a national origins quota. Each nationality was allotted visas equal to 2 percent of the number of people of that nationality in the United States in the 1890 census, a formula designed to favor immigrants from northern and western Europe and to cut immigration from southern and eastern Europe. The law also barred virtually all immigration from Asia. The quota system it created remained the main way the United States selected immigrants until 1965.
thumbAlt: Newspaper headline about the Immigration Act of 1924

title: The Kansas-Nebraska Act
subtitle: The law that repealed the Missouri Compromise and set Kansas bleeding, 1854
summary: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 created the territories of Kansas and Nebraska and let their settlers decide whether to allow slavery, repealing the Missouri Compromise, which had banned slavery there. Proslavery and antislavery settlers rushed into Kansas, and the conflict turned so violent it became known as “Bleeding Kansas.” Outrage over the act led to the founding of the Republican Party and pushed the country closer to civil war.
thumbAlt: Historical map showing territories after the Kansas-Nebraska Act

title: The Mayflower Compact
subtitle: Passengers bound for Virginia agree to govern themselves at Plymouth
summary: Before going ashore in November 1620, the male passengers of the Mayflower signed a short agreement to “covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick” and to obey the laws that body would make. They had landed far north of the Virginia territory their patent covered, so they had no legal charter for where they were. The Mayflower Compact became the basis of government at Plymouth Colony and an early example of self-government by mutual consent.
thumbAlt: Painting of the Pilgrims signing the Mayflower Compact

title: The Monroe Doctrine
subtitle: The United States warns Europe away from the Americas, 1823
summary: In his annual message to Congress on December 2, 1823, President James Monroe declared that the Americas were “henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers,” and that the United States would stay out of European affairs. Largely the work of Secretary of State John Quincy Adams, the policy aimed to protect newly independent Latin American republics. Over time it became the cornerstone of U.S. policy in the hemisphere, and a justification for U.S. intervention there.
thumbAlt: Political cartoon of Uncle Sam enforcing the Monroe Doctrine

title: The Nineteenth Amendment
subtitle: Women’s right to vote, 1920
summary: The Nineteenth Amendment provides that “the right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.” First introduced in Congress in 1878, it passed in June 1919 and was ratified on August 18, 1920, when Tennessee became the thirty-sixth state to approve it. It capped more than seventy years of organizing that began at Seneca Falls in 1848, and it was widely called the “Susan B. Anthony Amendment.” Discriminatory state laws, however, kept many women of color from voting long afterward.
thumbAlt: The Nineteenth Amendment

title: The Northwest Ordinance
subtitle: The plan for governing the Old Northwest and admitting new states
summary: Passed by the Confederation Congress in July 1787, the Northwest Ordinance set out how the territory north of the Ohio River would be governed and how it would become new states equal to the original thirteen. It guaranteed basic rights to settlers, encouraged education, and banned slavery in the territory. Its promise of “utmost good faith” toward Native nations was broken almost immediately.
location: Territory northwest of the Ohio River (present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota)
thumbAlt: Map of the Northwest Territory

title: Social Security Act
subtitle: The 1935 law that created old-age pensions and unemployment insurance
summary: Signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on August 14, 1935, the Social Security Act created a national system of old-age benefits for workers, funded by taxes on wages and payrolls, along with unemployment insurance and aid to dependent children, people who are blind, and people with disabilities. It was the centerpiece of the Second New Deal and the foundation of the American safety net, though at first it excluded farm and domestic workers, a policy that disproportionately affected African Americans.
thumbAlt: President Franklin D. Roosevelt signing the Social Security Act

title: The Thirteenth Amendment
subtitle: The constitutional abolition of slavery, 1865
summary: The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery throughout the United States. Passed by Congress on January 31, 1865, and ratified on December 6, 1865, it declares that “neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States.” It completed the work of the Emancipation Proclamation, which had freed enslaved people only in Confederate territory, and it freed some four million people. It was the first of the three Reconstruction amendments. Its exception for criminal punishment, and the Black Codes that followed, showed that the end of legal slavery did not end racial injustice.
thumbAlt: The Thirteenth Amendment

title: Voting Rights Act of 1965
subtitle: The law that enforced the Fifteenth Amendment
summary: The Voting Rights Act of 1965, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson on August 6, 1965, was “an act to enforce the fifteenth amendment,” passed ninety-five years after that amendment was ratified. It outlawed literacy tests and sent federal examiners to register voters in places with a history of discrimination. Its Section 5 required those places to get federal approval, called “preclearance,” before changing their voting rules. Congress acted after the violence of the Selma voting rights campaign, above all the attack on marchers on “Bloody Sunday,” March 7, 1965. Within months a quarter of a million new Black voters had registered. The Archives calls it the most significant change in federal–state relations over voting since Reconstruction.
thumbAlt: President Lyndon Johnson signing the Voting Rights Act

title: The Overthrow and Annexation of Hawaiʻi
subtitle: How American sugar planters toppled Queen Liliʻuokalani and the United States took the islands in 1898
summary: In the nineteenth century the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi came to be dominated by American missionaries, businessmen, and sugar planters. In 1887 armed businessmen forced King Kalākaua to accept the “Bayonet Constitution,” and on January 17, 1893, with the support of the U.S. minister and Marines from the USS Boston, they overthrew his sister, Queen Liliʻuokalani. A U.S. investigation found the overthrow illegal, and more than half of Native Hawaiians signed a petition against annexation. But during the Spanish-American War, Congress annexed the islands by joint resolution, signed on July 7, 1898. Hawaiʻi became the fiftieth state in 1959.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Liliʻuokalani, the last monarch of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, around 1891

title: Apollo 11
subtitle: The first human landing on the Moon, July 1969
summary: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle on the Moon’s Sea of Tranquility while Michael Collins orbited overhead in the command module Columbia. An estimated 650 million people watched as Armstrong stepped onto the surface, describing it as “one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind.” The mission fulfilled President Kennedy’s 1961 goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth, and it was a triumph for the United States in the space race with the Soviet Union.
location: Launched from Cape Kennedy, Florida; landed in the Sea of Tranquility on the Moon
thumbAlt: Buzz Aldrin standing on the Moon in his spacesuit

title: Atomic Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
subtitle: The first and only use of nuclear weapons in war, August 1945
summary: On August 6, 1945, an American B-29 bomber dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, Japan; three days later a second bomb struck Nagasaki. Some 70,000 people probably died immediately at Hiroshima, and more than 100,000 by the end of 1945; the best estimate at Nagasaki is 40,000 initial deaths. Japan announced its surrender on August 15. The bombings ended World War II and opened the nuclear age, and whether they were necessary remains one of the most debated questions in American history.
thumbAlt: Mushroom clouds over Hiroshima and Nagasaki

title: The Battle of Gettysburg
subtitle: The bloodiest battle of the Civil War, July 1–3, 1863
summary: For three days in July 1863, the Union Army of the Potomac under George G. Meade and Robert E. Lee’s Confederate Army of Northern Virginia fought around the Pennsylvania town of Gettysburg. With as many as 51,000 soldiers killed, wounded, captured, or missing, it was the bloodiest battle of the war. Lee’s defeat, capped by the failed assault known as Pickett’s Charge, ended his second invasion of the North and is often called the turning point of the Civil War.
thumbAlt: Lithograph of Pickett’s Charge at the Battle of Gettysburg

title: The Battle of the Little Bighorn
subtitle: Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors destroy Custer’s command, June 1876
summary: On June 25–26, 1876, warriors of the Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho defeated the U.S. 7th Cavalry along the Little Bighorn River in Montana, killing Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer and every soldier in the five companies under his immediate command. The battle, which Native people call the Battle of the Greasy Grass, was a stunning victory for the nations resisting confinement to reservations, but a short-lived one. Within a year most had surrendered, and the government seized the sacred Black Hills.
thumbAlt: Pictorial account of the Battle of the Little Bighorn by White Swan

title: The Alamo and the Texas Revolution
subtitle: The thirteen-day siege of 1836 and the war that made Texas an independent republic
summary: In February 1836, during the Texas Revolution against Mexico, a small garrison of Texan and American volunteers held the old Alamo mission at San Antonio against the army of Mexican president Antonio López de Santa Anna. After a thirteen-day siege, some 1,800 Mexican troops stormed the walls before dawn on March 6; within ninety minutes every defender, including William Barret Travis, Jim Bowie, and Davy Crockett, was dead. Six weeks later Sam Houston’s army routed Santa Anna at San Jacinto, and Texas won its independence as a republic that protected slavery.
location: San Antonio de Béxar, Mexican Texas
thumbAlt: Robert Jenkins Onderdonk’s painting The Fall of the Alamo, about 1903, showing Davy Crockett swinging his rifle as Mexican soldiers storm the mission

title: Bonnie and Clyde
subtitle: Depression-era outlaws whose short, violent crime spree became an American legend
summary: Bonnie Parker and Clyde Barrow were young Texans who, from 1932 to 1934, robbed grocery stores, filling stations, and small banks across the Southwest and Midwest and killed a number of people, several of them law officers. A posse led by former Texas Ranger Frank Hamer killed them in a roadside ambush in Louisiana on May 23, 1934. Small-time criminals in life, they became one of America’s most enduring legends, above all through the 1967 film Bonnie and Clyde.
location: Texas, the Southwest, and the Midwest
thumbAlt: Bonnie Parker leaning on Clyde Barrow’s shoulder as they pose in front of a car, about 1933

title: The Boston Massacre
subtitle: British soldiers fire into a Boston crowd, killing five, in March 1770
summary: On the evening of March 5, 1770, a crowd confronted a small group of British soldiers outside the Custom House on King Street in Boston. Taunted and pelted with snowballs, ice, and sticks, the soldiers fired, killing five men, among them Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Indigenous ancestry, and wounding six. Patriots called it a massacre of civilians; loyalists called it self-defense against a mob. John Adams defended the soldiers in court and won acquittals for most of them, but the killings became one of the most powerful stories of the coming Revolution.
thumbAlt: Paul Revere’s 1770 engraving “The Bloody Massacre,” showing a line of British soldiers firing on a crowd on King Street

title: The Boston Tea Party
subtitle: Colonists destroy East India Company tea in Boston Harbor
summary: On the night of December 16, 1773, colonists disguised as Indians boarded East India Company ships in Boston Harbor and dumped the East India Company’s tea into the water. The protest targeted a law that gave the company a monopoly on tea shipments to the colonies. Britain’s harsh response, closing the port of Boston and curtailing self-government in Massachusetts, pushed the colonies toward united resistance and, within two years, war.
thumbAlt: Currier print of colonists dumping tea into Boston Harbor

title: The California Gold Rush
subtitle: The 1848 discovery at Sutter’s Mill that sent fortune seekers flooding west
summary: On January 24, 1848, James W. Marshall, building a sawmill for John Sutter on the South Fork of the American River, found gold. Fortune seekers, mostly young men, poured in from the eastern states and from around the world, and San Francisco grew from about five hundred people to almost fifty thousand in five years. Few miners got rich, but within two years California had applied to join the Union as a free state; the rush brought violence against Native Americans and long-established Mexican communities, and drew immigrants from China.
location: Coloma and the Sierra Nevada foothills, California
thumbAlt: Daguerreotype of California gold miners working a long tom sluice, about 1850–1852

title: The Voyages of Columbus
subtitle: Spanish-sponsored voyages that began sustained contact between Europe and the Americas
summary: On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus, a Genoese sailor seeking a western sea route to Asia on behalf of Spain, landed on an island in the Bahamas that its Lucayan inhabitants called Guanahani. His four voyages did not reach Asia, but they began permanent contact between Europe and the Americas, setting off the Columbian Exchange, Spanish conquest and colonization, and a catastrophe for the Taíno and other Indigenous peoples of the Caribbean.
location: The Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, and the Caribbean
thumbAlt: Map of the four voyages of Columbus

title: The Compromise of 1850
subtitle: Congress tries to settle the slavery question after the Mexican War
summary: The lands taken from Mexico forced Congress to decide whether slavery could spread west. In 1850, after seven months of debate, Congress passed five laws: California entered as a free state; New Mexico and Utah territories would decide on slavery themselves; the slave trade (but not slavery) was abolished in Washington, D.C.; a Texas boundary dispute was settled; and a harsh new Fugitive Slave Act required people in free states to help capture freedom seekers. The compromise postponed disunion but deepened Northern anger over slavery.
thumbAlt: Engraving of the U.S. Senate in session in 1850

title: The Disputed Election of 1876 and the End of Reconstruction
subtitle: The “Compromise of 1877”
summary: The presidential election of 1876 between Republican Rutherford B. Hayes and Democrat Samuel J. Tilden produced disputed returns in three Southern states and Oregon. Tilden led the popular vote by about 250,000 but was one electoral vote short. Congress created a special Electoral Commission, which awarded all the disputed votes to Hayes. As Democrats threatened to obstruct the count, Hayes’s allies and Southern Democrats negotiated, and Hayes withdrew the federal troops protecting the last Republican governments in the South. The settlement, often called the Compromise of 1877, marked the end of Reconstruction.
location: Washington, D.C.; Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina, and Oregon
thumbAlt: Political cartoon about the disputed election of 1876

title: The Constitutional Convention
subtitle: Fifty-five delegates meet in secret to redesign the American government
summary: In the summer of 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia, officially to revise the Articles of Confederation. Instead, they wrote an entirely new Constitution. Working in secret, they argued over how to represent large and small states, how much power to give a national government, and how to count enslaved people, and settled each dispute through compromise. The document they signed on September 17 still governs the United States.
thumbAlt: Howard Chandler Christy’s painting of the signing of the Constitution

title: COVID-19 Pandemic
subtitle: The coronavirus pandemic in the United States, 2020–2023
summary: COVID-19, a disease caused by a new coronavirus first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019, reached the United States in January 2020. Schools, offices, and businesses shut down; millions lost their jobs; and hospitals were overwhelmed. Vaccines developed at record speed became available in December 2020, but the virus kept spreading in new variants, and responses to masks and vaccines became politically polarized. By May 2022, more than one million Americans had died.
thumbAlt: Electron microscope image of the SARS-CoV-2 virus that causes COVID-19

title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
subtitle: The October 1962 showdown in which the superpowers came closest to nuclear war
summary: In October 1962 an American U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet nuclear missile sites under construction in Cuba. In the days that followed, President John F. Kennedy and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev faced each other in the most dangerous confrontation of the Cold War, the moment when the two superpowers came closest to nuclear conflict. Kennedy imposed a naval “quarantine” of the island; Khrushchev finally agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for an American pledge not to invade Cuba, and a secret promise to pull U.S. missiles out of Turkey.
thumbAlt: U.S. aerial reconnaissance photograph of a Soviet medium-range ballistic missile launch site at San Cristobal, Cuba, November 1, 1962

title: D-Day
subtitle: The Allied invasion of Normandy, June 6, 1944
summary: On June 6, 1944, nearly 160,000 American, British, Canadian, and other Allied troops landed along fifty miles of the heavily fortified Normandy coast of France, supported by more than 5,000 ships and 13,000 aircraft. Called Operation Overlord and commanded by General Dwight D. Eisenhower, it was the largest amphibious assault in history. More than 9,000 Allied soldiers were killed or wounded that day, but the Allies gained a foothold in western Europe that led to the liberation of France and the defeat of Nazi Germany.
thumbAlt: American soldiers wading ashore from a landing craft on Omaha Beach

title: The Dust Bowl
subtitle: Drought, dust storms, and migration on the southern Plains in the 1930s
summary: During the 1930s, years of drought combined with farming practices that had stripped the Great Plains of its protective grass, and high winds lifted the exposed soil into enormous dust storms. The worst-hit area (the western third of Kansas, southeastern Colorado, the Oklahoma Panhandle, most of the Texas Panhandle, and northeastern New Mexico) became known as the Dust Bowl. Farms failed, hundreds of thousands of people left the region, and the disaster pushed the federal government to promote soil conservation.
location: Southern Great Plains: western Kansas, southeastern Colorado, the Oklahoma Panhandle, the Texas Panhandle, and northeastern New Mexico
thumbAlt: A wall of dust approaching a town in Texas in 1935

title: The Election of 1800
subtitle: The first transfer of power between rival parties
summary: In 1800 the Democratic-Republicans under Thomas Jefferson defeated President John Adams and the Federalists in a bitter campaign fought largely in partisan newspapers. A flaw in the Constitution produced a tie between Jefferson and his own running mate, Aaron Burr, throwing the decision to the House of Representatives, which deadlocked through thirty-five ballots before choosing Jefferson. The result was the first peaceful transfer of power from one party to another in the United States.
location: Nationwide; decided in the House of Representatives, Washington, D.C.
thumbAlt: Campaign banner celebrating Thomas Jefferson

title: The End of the Cold War
subtitle: The fall of communism in Eastern Europe and the collapse of the Soviet Union, 1989–1991
summary: Between 1989 and 1991, the communist regimes of Eastern Europe collapsed one after another, the Berlin Wall fell, and the Soviet Union itself dissolved. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev’s reforms, perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness), and his decision not to use force to prop up allied regimes made peaceful change possible. Presidents Ronald Reagan and George H. W. Bush combined pressure with negotiation. On December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned and the Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin, leaving the United States the world’s only superpower.
location: Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union
thumbAlt: East and West Germans at the Brandenburg Gate in 1989

title: The Erie Canal
subtitle: The 363-mile “artificial river” that linked the Great Lakes to New York City in 1825
summary: Built between 1817 and 1825, the Erie Canal ran 363 miles across upstate New York from Albany on the Hudson River to Buffalo on Lake Erie. Dug largely by hand, climbing hills through 83 locks, it was the longest artificial waterway and the greatest public works project in North America. It cut shipping costs by 90 percent, opened the interior of the continent to settlers and trade, made New York City the nation’s leading port and financial center, and launched a national canal-building boom.
thumbAlt: 1839 engraving of the Erie Canal at Lockport, New York, after a picture by W. H. Bartlett

title: The First Africans in Virginia
subtitle: 1619: Enslaved Angolans arrive at Point Comfort
summary: In late August 1619, the English privateer White Lion arrived at Point Comfort, Virginia, and traded about twenty Africans for food; the ship Treasurer soon brought a few more. They had been captured in west central Africa, most likely from the kingdom of Ndongo in present-day Angola, and taken from a Portuguese slave ship bound for Mexico. They were the first documented Africans in English Virginia, and their arrival is often taken as the beginning of the history of slavery in what became the United States.
thumbAlt: Howard Pyle’s 1901 illustration imagining the arrival of Africans at Jamestown in 1619

title: The Great Depression
subtitle: The deepest economic collapse in American history, 1929–1941
summary: The Great Depression was the longest and deepest economic downturn in the history of the United States and the modern industrial economy. Beginning in 1929, it brought a stock market crash, thousands of bank failures, collapsing farm prices, and unemployment that reached about a quarter of the workforce. The Federal Reserve’s own historians now say its mistakes made the slump far worse. Herbert Hoover’s reliance on voluntary action gave way to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, which transformed the federal government, but full recovery came only with World War II.
thumbAlt: Dorothea Lange’s photograph Migrant Mother

title: The Great Recession
subtitle: The financial crisis and deep recession of 2007–2009
summary: The Great Recession began in December 2007 and ended in June 2009, the longest recession since World War II. It grew out of a housing bubble fueled by risky “subprime” mortgages that were bundled into securities and sold throughout the financial system. When homeowners began to default, major financial firms such as Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers collapsed. Home prices fell about 30 percent, stocks fell 57 percent, and unemployment peaked at 10 percent. The federal government and the Federal Reserve intervened on a massive scale to stabilize the financial system.
thumbAlt: Lehman Brothers headquarters in New York City on September 15, 2008, the month the firm filed for bankruptcy

title: The Great Society
subtitle: Lyndon Johnson’s program to end poverty and racial injustice, 1964–1968
summary: The Great Society was President Lyndon B. Johnson’s sweeping program of domestic reform. Announced in a May 1964 speech calling for “an end to poverty and racial injustice,” it produced the most ambitious burst of legislation since the New Deal: the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid, federal aid to education, food stamps, the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts, and an immigration law that abolished the national-origins quotas of 1924. Much of it remains in place today.
thumbAlt: President Lyndon Johnson signing the Medicare bill with Harry Truman beside him

title: The Haymarket Affair
subtitle: A bomb at a Chicago labor rally, May 4, 1886
summary: On May 4, 1886, about 1,500 workers rallied near Chicago’s Haymarket Square to protest police violence against strikers the day before, during a nationwide campaign for the eight-hour day. As police moved to disperse the crowd, someone threw a bomb; police and possibly others opened fire. Seven police officers and at least one civilian died. Eight anarchists were convicted of murder on little evidence linking them to the bomb; four were hanged. The affair set off a wave of anti-labor and anti-immigrant fear.
thumbAlt: Harper’s Weekly engraving of the Haymarket bombing

title: Independence Day (the Fourth of July)
subtitle: The nation’s birthday, celebrated since 1776 and a federal holiday since 1870
summary: Independence Day marks July 4, 1776, when the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. John Adams predicted the day of independence would be celebrated “with Pomp and Parade… Bonfires and Illuminations from one End of this Continent to the other,” and Americans have marked it ever since with parades, music, and public readings of the Declaration. Congress made it one of the first four federal holidays in 1870. It has also been a day for Americans to measure the nation against its founding promise, most famously in Frederick Douglass’s 1852 speech “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”
location: Nationwide; the Declaration was adopted in Philadelphia
thumbAlt: John Lewis Krimmel’s painting of a crowded Fourth of July celebration in Philadelphia’s Centre Square, around 1812

title: Indian Removal
subtitle: The forced expulsion of Native nations from the East, 1830–1850
summary: Indian removal was the federal policy of forcing Native nations east of the Mississippi River to give up their homelands and move to “Indian Territory” in what is now Oklahoma. President Andrew Jackson made it a central goal, and Congress passed the Indian Removal Act on May 28, 1830. Through coerced treaties, bribery, and the army, the government relocated about 100,000 people between 1830 and 1850, among them the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee Creek, and Seminole nations. The best-known removal, the Cherokee Trail of Tears of 1838–1839, killed thousands. Removal opened millions of acres of rich land east of the Mississippi to white settlers.
location: The Southeast and Old Northwest to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma)
thumbAlt: Map of the forced removal routes of the Five Tribes

title: The Founding of Jamestown
subtitle: The first permanent English settlement in North America, 1607
summary: In May 1607, 104 English men and boys sent by the Virginia Company chose a marshy island on the James River for a settlement they named for King James I. Jamestown nearly failed, from disease, hunger, and conflict with the Powhatan peoples whose land it occupied, but survived to become the first permanent English settlement in North America. By 1619 it had brought together three continents: the first representative assembly, the first documented Africans, and tobacco grown for profit on Native land.
thumbAlt: Replicas of the ships that carried the Jamestown colonists

title: Japanese American Incarceration
subtitle: The forced removal and imprisonment of Japanese Americans during World War II
summary: After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, the United States government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from their homes on the West Coast and held them in camps for most of World War II. Nearly 70,000 of them were American citizens. None was charged with a crime, and none could appeal. The removal rested on Executive Order 9066, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on February 19, 1942, and the Supreme Court upheld it in Korematsu v. United States (1944). In 1988 Congress acknowledged that the incarceration was a “grave injustice” caused by “racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership.” It apologized and paid $20,000 to each survivor.
location: West Coast exclusion zones; ten War Relocation Centers in California, Arizona, Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and Arkansas
thumbAlt: Rows of barracks at the Manzanar War Relocation Center

title: Juneteenth
subtitle: June 19, 1865: freedom announced in Texas, now a national holiday
summary: On June 19, 1865, two and a half years after the Emancipation Proclamation, Union general Gordon Granger issued General Order No. 3 in Galveston, informing the people of Texas that all enslaved people were free. The day became known as Juneteenth, a blend of “June” and “nineteenth.” Celebrated by African American communities in Texas since 1866 and later in other states, it is the oldest known celebration of the end of slavery in the United States, and became a national holiday in 2021.
thumbAlt: The handwritten text of General Order No. 3, issued at Galveston, Texas, on June 19, 1865

title: The Lewis and Clark Expedition
subtitle: The Corps of Discovery crosses the continent, 1804–1806
summary: In 1804, at Thomas Jefferson’s direction, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led a small army unit, the Corps of Discovery, up the Missouri River and across the Rocky Mountains to the Pacific Ocean, returning to St. Louis in 1806. They mapped the West, recorded its plants and animals, and met dozens of Native nations. Their success depended on Native guides and hosts, above all on Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone woman, and on the labor of York, a man enslaved by Clark.
location: From St. Louis up the Missouri River, across the Rockies, to the Pacific coast and back
thumbAlt: Painting of Lewis and Clark’s party on the Columbia River

title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
subtitle: April 19, 1775: the first fighting of the American Revolution and “the shot heard ’round the world”
summary: Before dawn on April 19, 1775, some 700 British soldiers marched from Boston to seize the military supplies that Massachusetts patriots had stockpiled at Concord. Warned by Paul Revere, William Dawes, and other riders, local militia turned out. Shots were fired on Lexington Green (no one knows who fired first) and later at Concord’s North Bridge. On the long march back to Boston, thousands of militiamen fired on the British from behind trees, walls, and houses. By nightfall 49 colonists and 73 British soldiers were dead, and the American Revolutionary War had begun.
thumbAlt: Amos Doolittle’s 1775 engraving of British regulars firing on the militia on Lexington Green

title: The Assassination of Abraham Lincoln
subtitle: Ford’s Theatre, April 14, 1865
summary: On the evening of April 14, 1865, five days after Lee’s surrender at Appomattox, President Abraham Lincoln was shot in the head by the actor John Wilkes Booth while watching a play at Ford’s Theatre in Washington. He died the next morning, the first American president to be assassinated. Booth, a Confederate sympathizer, had plotted with others to kill several leaders of the government. Lincoln’s death turned the celebration of victory into national mourning and placed Andrew Johnson in charge of Reconstruction.
thumbAlt: Currier and Ives print of Lincoln’s assassination at Ford’s Theatre

title: The Little Rock Nine
subtitle: The desegregation of Central High School, 1957
summary: In September 1957, nine Black students tried to enroll at all-white Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, under a court-ordered desegregation plan. Governor Orval Faubus sent the Arkansas National Guard to keep them out, and a white mob gathered outside. After weeks of standoff, President Dwight D. Eisenhower sent troops of the Army’s 101st Airborne Division to escort and protect the students, a dramatic use of federal power to enforce Brown v. Board of Education.
thumbAlt: Members of the Little Rock Nine with New York mayor Robert F. Wagner

title: The Louisiana Purchase
subtitle: The United States doubles in size, 1803
summary: In 1803 the United States bought the vast Louisiana territory from France for $15 million, about 828,000 square miles between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains, for roughly four cents an acre. The purchase doubled the size of the country, gave it control of New Orleans and the Mississippi, and opened the way to westward expansion. It also raised hard questions: whether the Constitution allowed it, whether slavery would spread into the new lands, and what would become of the many Native nations who lived there.
location: The Mississippi River valley to the Rocky Mountains
thumbAlt: Map of the Louisiana Purchase within the present-day United States

title: March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom
subtitle: The 1963 march where King delivered “I Have a Dream”
summary: On August 28, 1963, a crowd that the King Institute puts at more than 200,000 and the National Archives at more than 250,000 gathered in Washington, D.C., for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Conceived by the labor leader A. Philip Randolph and organized by Bayard Rustin in less than two months, it united the major civil rights organizations, labor unions, and churches. They demanded a strong civil rights law, voting rights, school desegregation, jobs, and fair employment. It closed at the Lincoln Memorial with Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech. The march helped build pressure for the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, whose provisions reflected its demands.
thumbAlt: Martin Luther King Jr. among the crowd at the March on Washington

title: The Marshall Plan
subtitle: The European Recovery Program, 1948–1952
summary: The Marshall Plan was a massive American program to rebuild the war-ravaged economies of Western Europe after World War II. Proposed by Secretary of State George C. Marshall in a June 1947 speech at Harvard, it provided more than $12 billion between 1948 and 1952. American leaders saw it as both a humanitarian effort and a way to stop the spread of communism by restoring prosperity. The Soviet Union refused to take part and kept its Eastern European satellites out, deepening the division of Europe.
thumbAlt: Poster promoting the Marshall Plan

title: McCarthyism and the Second Red Scare
subtitle: Anticommunist investigations and accusations, late 1940s–1954
summary: In the early Cold War, fear of communist subversion swept the United States. Congressional committees, the FBI, loyalty boards, and private employers investigated thousands of Americans; many lost their jobs or were blacklisted for past political associations. The era takes its name from Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin, who from 1950 made sensational, unsupported charges that communists had infiltrated the government, until televised hearings in 1954 exposed his tactics and the Senate condemned him.
location: Washington, D.C., Hollywood, universities, unions, and communities nationwide
thumbAlt: Joseph Welch and Senator Joseph McCarthy at the Army-McCarthy hearings

title: The Missouri Compromise
subtitle: Congress balances slave and free states, 1820
summary: When Missouri asked to join the Union as a slave state in 1819, it set off the first great national crisis over slavery. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, preserving the balance between them in the Senate, and banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of latitude 36°30′. The line held for thirty-four years, but the crisis revealed how deeply slavery divided the nation. Thomas Jefferson called it “a fire bell in the night.”
thumbAlt: Map of free and slave territory under the Missouri Compromise

title: Montgomery Bus Boycott
subtitle: The thirteen-month protest that launched the modern civil rights movement
summary: The Montgomery bus boycott began on December 5, 1955, four days after Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. For 381 days Montgomery’s Black residents walked, shared rides, and organized carpools rather than ride segregated city buses. The protest was planned by the Women’s Political Council and E. D. Nixon and led by the Montgomery Improvement Association. Its president was a twenty-six-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr. It survived bombings, mass indictments, and court injunctions, and it ended in victory after the Supreme Court affirmed, in Browder v. Gayle, that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The boycott made King a national figure and showed that nonviolent mass protest could defeat Jim Crow.
thumbAlt: Rosa Parks being fingerprinted after her arrest during the Montgomery bus boycott

title: The New Deal
subtitle: Franklin D. Roosevelt’s programs of relief, recovery, and reform, 1933–1939
summary: The New Deal was President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s response to the Great Depression: a burst of federal programs to stabilize the banks, put the unemployed to work, raise farm prices, protect workers’ right to organize, and create a safety net for the elderly and the jobless. It did not end the Depression, and it left racial and gender inequalities largely in place. But it transformed the role of the federal government and the presidency, and it built a Democratic coalition that dominated politics for a generation.
thumbAlt: Collage of New Deal programs and posters

title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
subtitle: Japan’s surprise attack that brought the United States into World War II
summary: On the morning of December 7, 1941, Japanese planes attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. In less than two hours the fleet was devastated and more than 3,500 Americans were killed or wounded, about 2,400 of them killed. The next day President Franklin D. Roosevelt called December 7 “a date which will live in infamy,” and Congress declared war on Japan. The attack ended American isolationism and brought the United States into World War II.
thumbAlt: The battleship USS Arizona burning after the Japanese attack

title: The Peopling of the Americas
subtitle: How and when the first people arrived, a question science is still answering
summary: People have lived in the Americas for well over twenty thousand years. For much of the twentieth century, scientists believed the first arrivals came roughly 13,000 years ago, walking from Asia across a land bridge exposed by low Ice Age seas. Newer evidence, above all human footprints preserved at White Sands, New Mexico, and dated to about 23,000–21,000 years ago, has pushed that date much earlier. How and when people first came remains one of the liveliest questions in archaeology.
location: Beringia, the Pacific coast, and the interior of North America
thumbAlt: Map of possible routes of the first peopling of the Americas through Beringia

title: Plymouth Colony and the Wampanoag
subtitle: The Pilgrims’ settlement and the alliance that kept it alive, 1620–1621
summary: In December 1620, English colonists from the Mayflower, many of them religious Separatists later called Pilgrims, settled at Plymouth, in the homeland of the Wampanoag people. Half of them died that first winter. In March 1621, the Wampanoag leader Massasoit, whose people had been devastated by diseases brought by earlier English visitors and who faced pressure from the rival Narragansett, made an alliance with the newcomers. That treaty kept the colony alive, and Massasoit honored it for the rest of his life.
location: Plymouth, Massachusetts, in the homeland of the Wampanoag
thumbAlt: Engraving of Plymouth governor John Carver meeting the Wampanoag leader Massasoit

title: Prohibition
subtitle: The national ban on alcohol, 1920–1933
summary: Prohibition was the nationwide ban on making, selling, and transporting alcoholic beverages, imposed by the Eighteenth Amendment and in force from January 1920 until its repeal by the Twenty-first Amendment in December 1933. The culmination of a century-long temperance crusade, it cut drinking but proved extremely hard to enforce. Bootlegging, speakeasies, and organized crime flourished, and in 1933 the Twenty-first Amendment repealed it.
thumbAlt: Prohibition agents destroying barrels of alcohol

title: The Pueblo Revolt
subtitle: Pueblo nations unite to drive Spanish colonizers out of New Mexico, 1680
summary: In August 1680, the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico, speaking several languages and living in dozens of separate towns, rose together against eight decades of Spanish rule. Organized by a religious leader from San Juan Pueblo named Po’Pay, the coordinated revolt killed missionaries and colonists, besieged Santa Fe, and drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for twelve years, one of the most successful Native uprisings against European colonization in North American history.
location: Santa Fe and the Pueblos of the upper Rio Grande, New Mexico
thumbAlt: Loren Mozley’s 1936 mural of the Pueblo Revolt

title: Puerto Rico Under the United States
subtitle: From Spanish colony to U.S. territory and commonwealth, 1898–1952
summary: Puerto Rico, long a Spanish colony, passed to the United States in 1898 at the end of the Spanish-American War. After two years of military rule, the Foraker Act of 1900 set up a civil government but gave Puerto Ricans no U.S. citizenship. Island leaders such as Luis Muñoz Rivera pressed Congress for years, and the Jones-Shafroth Act of March 2, 1917, made Puerto Ricans U.S. citizens. In 1952 Puerto Rico became a self-governing commonwealth. Its people are citizens, yet the island is represented in Congress only by a non-voting resident commissioner, and the nature of that relationship is still debated today.
thumbAlt: Members of Puerto Rico’s first autonomous cabinet under Spain, including Luis Muñoz Rivera, as published in 1898

title: The Pullman Strike
subtitle: A national railroad boycott crushed by federal troops, 1894
summary: In May 1894, during a severe depression, workers at George Pullman’s sleeping-car factory near Chicago struck after he cut wages by a quarter while keeping rents in his company town unchanged. The American Railway Union, led by Eugene V. Debs, launched a national boycott of trains carrying Pullman cars, halting rail traffic across much of the country. A federal court injunction and thousands of federal troops broke the strike, Debs went to jail, and the union was destroyed.
location: Pullman, Illinois (Chicago), and rail lines nationwide
thumbAlt: Strikers outside the Arcade Building in Pullman, Illinois

title: Reconstruction
subtitle: The struggle to rebuild the Union and define freedom after the Civil War
summary: Reconstruction was the era in which the United States tried to reunite the nation after the Civil War and decide what freedom would mean for four million formerly enslaved people. Congress wrote the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments into the Constitution, abolishing slavery, making Black Americans citizens, and forbidding racial discrimination in voting. Black Southerners built schools and churches, searched for lost family members, voted, and held office, as many as 2,000 of them. Terrorist violence, economic depression, and Northern retreat brought Reconstruction to an end by 1877, opening the way to Jim Crow.
location: The former Confederate states and the nation
thumbAlt: Currier and Ives print of the first Black members of Congress, including Senator Hiram Revels

title: The Roanoke Colony
subtitle: England’s “Lost Colony,” 1587
summary: Sponsored by Sir Walter Raleigh, England’s first attempts at a colony in North America centered on Roanoke Island in present-day North Carolina between 1584 and 1590. The last group, 118 men, women, and children led by John White, arrived in 1587. When White returned with supplies three years later, the settlers were gone, leaving the word “CROATOAN” carved into a post. What became of them has never been solved.
thumbAlt: Artist’s reconstruction of the fort at Roanoke Island

title: The Salem Witch Trials
subtitle: The 1692 witch hunt in Puritan Massachusetts that sent twenty people to their deaths
summary: In 1692 a panic over witchcraft swept Salem Village and neighboring towns in Puritan Massachusetts. It began when two girls in the household of the village minister fell into fits and three women were arrested for bewitching them; within months hundreds of people had been accused. A special court, relying on “spectral evidence” (testimony that an accused person’s spirit had tormented the victims), sentenced people to death. Nineteen people were hanged and one man was pressed to death with stones before the governor shut the court down. The trials became America’s most famous warning against mass hysteria and false accusation.
location: Salem Village (now Danvers), Salem Town, Andover, and nearby towns, Massachusetts
thumbAlt: T. H. Matteson’s 1855 painting of the 1692 witchcraft trial of George Jacobs in Salem, with an accuser pointing at the old man

title: Selma to Montgomery Marches
subtitle: “Bloody Sunday” and the march for voting rights, 1965
summary: In early 1965, local activists, SNCC, and Martin Luther King Jr.’s SCLC campaigned for voting rights in Selma, Alabama, where only 2 percent of Black residents were registered. On March 7, remembered as “Bloody Sunday,” state troopers and local lawmen attacked peaceful marchers with clubs and tear gas at the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Televised images shocked the nation. Two weeks later, under federal protection, thousands marched the 54 miles to Montgomery. The campaign led directly to the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
thumbAlt: Marchers on the Selma to Montgomery march

title: The Seneca Falls Convention
subtitle: The first women’s rights convention, July 1848
summary: On July 19 and 20, 1848, about three hundred women and men met at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, for the first women’s rights convention in the United States. Organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, it adopted a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence. It proclaimed that “all men and women are created equal” and listed the wrongs done to women, beginning with the denial of the vote. One hundred people signed it, 68 women and 32 men. Frederick Douglass was among those who attended. The demand for the vote was the most controversial of its resolutions, and it launched the movement that won the Nineteenth Amendment seventy-two years later.
location: Wesleyan Chapel, Seneca Falls, New York
thumbAlt: The Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, where the 1848 convention met, now part of Women’s Rights National Historical Park

title: September 11 Attacks
subtitle: The al-Qaeda terrorist attacks of 2001
summary: On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four passenger planes. Two struck the towers of the World Trade Center in New York, which collapsed; one struck the Pentagon outside Washington; and the fourth, United Flight 93, crashed in a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought back. Nearly 3,000 people were killed. The attacks led to the war in Afghanistan, a global “war on terror,” and the Iraq War, and reshaped American security and foreign policy.
location: New York City; Arlington, Virginia; near Shanksville, Pennsylvania
thumbAlt: Smoke rising from the World Trade Center behind the Statue of Liberty

title: Shays’ Rebellion
subtitle: An armed uprising of indebted farmers that shook the new nation
summary: In 1786 and 1787, farmers in western Massachusetts, many of them Revolutionary War veterans, rose against state taxes and debt collection that threatened to cost them their farms. Led in part by Daniel Shays, a former Continental Army captain, they shut down courts and in January 1787 tried to seize the federal arsenal at Springfield. The militia scattered them, but the uprising alarmed national leaders and became a powerful argument for a stronger central government.
thumbAlt: Illustration of Shays’s forces fleeing troops at Springfield

title: Siege of Yorktown
subtitle: The 1781 American and French victory that effectively won the Revolutionary War
summary: In the fall of 1781 George Washington’s Continental Army and a French army under the Comte de Rochambeau marched hundreds of miles south to trap the British army of Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, while a French fleet under the Comte de Grasse blocked any rescue by sea. After a three-week siege, including a daring night attack in which Alexander Hamilton’s men stormed a British fort with unloaded muskets and fixed bayonets, Cornwallis surrendered on October 19. The British prime minister reacted, “Oh God. It is all over.” Fighting wound down, and the Treaty of Paris recognized American independence in 1783.
thumbAlt: Auguste Couder’s 1836 painting of Washington and Rochambeau giving their last orders before the attack at Yorktown

title: The Space Race
subtitle: From Sputnik to the moon: the Cold War contest for supremacy in space, 1957–1969
summary: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the world’s first artificial satellite, a beach-ball-sized sphere that circled Earth every ninety-eight minutes. Americans were shocked: if the Soviets could put a satellite in orbit, they could surely send nuclear missiles across the ocean. The Cold War rivalry moved into space. The United States answered with its own satellite, created NASA, and, after the Soviets put the first human in orbit in 1961, President John F. Kennedy pledged to land an American on the moon by the end of the decade, a goal reached with Apollo 11 in July 1969.
thumbAlt: William Pickering, James Van Allen, and Wernher von Braun hold up a model of Explorer 1, America’s first satellite, in 1958

title: The Stamp Act Crisis
subtitle: The first great colonial protest against taxation by Parliament
summary: In 1765 Parliament required colonists to buy government-issued stamps for newspapers, legal documents, and other paper goods. The tax was small, but the principle was enormous: colonists insisted that only their own elected assemblies could tax them. Protest united the colonies for the first time, through resolutions, a congress of nine colonies, boycotts, and crowd actions, and Parliament repealed the act within a year.
thumbAlt: Bostonians reading news of the Stamp Act

title: Stock Market Crash of 1929
subtitle: The collapse that ended the Roaring Twenties boom
summary: In October 1929 the great stock market boom of the 1920s collapsed. After panic selling on “Black Thursday,” October 24, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell nearly 13 percent on Black Monday, October 28, and nearly 12 percent more on Black Tuesday, October 29. The slide continued until 1932, when stocks had lost 89 percent of their peak value. The crash did not by itself cause the Great Depression, but it frightened investors and consumers and exposed deep weaknesses in the economy.
location: New York Stock Exchange, New York City
thumbAlt: Crowd gathered outside the New York Stock Exchange in October 1929

title: Thanksgiving Day
subtitle: How a day of thanks became a fixed national holiday, from Washington to Roosevelt
summary: Thanksgiving became a national custom by presidential proclamation. In 1789 the first Federal Congress asked George Washington to recommend a day of thanksgiving, and he named Thursday, November 26.
