Later presidents chose varying dates until Abraham Lincoln’s 1863 proclamation made the last Thursday of November the regular day. When Franklin D. Roosevelt moved it a week earlier in 1939, the country briefly celebrated two Thanksgivings until Congress fixed the holiday on the fourth Thursday of November in 1941.
thumbAlt: George Washington’s printed Thanksgiving Day proclamation of October 3, 1789

title: The Trail of Tears
subtitle: The forced removal of the Cherokee Nation, 1838–1839
summary: In 1838 federal troops and state militia forced about 16,000 Cherokee people from their homes in the Southeast into stockades, then sent them west to Indian Territory. Traveling by water and over land through the fall and winter of 1838–39, they suffered from disease, exposure, and hunger. About 4,000 died. The Trail of Tears has become the most widely known symbol of Indian removal.
location: From the Cherokee homeland in Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Alabama to Indian Territory (Oklahoma)
thumbAlt: Map of the forced removal routes of the Five Tribes

title: The Transcontinental Railroad
subtitle: Rails across the continent, 1863–1869
summary: The first transcontinental railroad linked the existing rail network of the East with the Pacific coast in 1869, cutting a journey of several months to about a week. Built with massive federal land grants and loans authorized by the Pacific Railway Act of 1862, it was the work of two companies and tens of thousands of laborers: Irish, German, and Italian immigrants building west from Omaha, and more than 10,000 Chinese workers building east from Sacramento. It transformed the national economy and accelerated the conquest of the West and its Native peoples.
location: Omaha, Nebraska, to Sacramento, California; joined at Promontory Summit, Utah
thumbAlt: Crews celebrating the completion of the transcontinental railroad at Promontory Summit

title: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
subtitle: A disaster that changed American workplace safety, March 25, 1911
summary: Near closing time on Saturday, March 25, 1911, fire swept the Triangle Waist Company, a blouse factory on the top floors of the Asch Building in Manhattan. It killed 146 of its roughly 500 workers, most of them young Italian and Jewish immigrant women, some only fourteen. On the ninth floor workers found the stairway doors locked or blocked, the fire escape gave way, and the fire department’s ladders could not reach them. Dozens jumped to their deaths in front of crowds on the street. The owners were acquitted of manslaughter. But public anger led New York to create a Factory Investigating Commission, whose work rewrote the state’s labor laws and shaped the career of a future Secretary of Labor, Frances Perkins.
location: Asch Building, Greenwich Village, New York City
thumbAlt: Smoke pouring from the building during the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire

title: Tulsa Race Massacre
subtitle: The destruction of Tulsa’s Greenwood District, 1921
summary: Over about eighteen hours on May 31 and June 1, 1921, white mobs attacked and burned the Greenwood District, the center of Black life in Tulsa, Oklahoma. More than a thousand homes and businesses were destroyed, and credible estimates of the dead range from fifty to three hundred. The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History calls it the single worst incident of racial violence in American history. No white person was ever imprisoned, and the massacre was long treated as an unspoken subject.
thumbAlt: Ruins of Tulsa’s Greenwood District after the 1921 massacre

title: The Watergate Scandal
subtitle: The abuses of power that forced President Nixon to resign, 1972–1974
summary: On June 17, 1972, five men were arrested breaking into the Democratic National Committee offices at the Watergate complex in Washington. One worked for President Richard Nixon’s reelection committee. The White House launched a cover-up, but journalists, a Senate committee, special prosecutors, and the courts gradually exposed a pattern of abuses of power. When the Supreme Court ordered Nixon to release his secret tapes, including one showing he had tried to use the CIA to block the FBI’s investigation, his support collapsed. Facing impeachment, Nixon became the first and only president to resign, on August 9, 1974.
thumbAlt: Richard Nixon waving from the steps of a helicopter as he leaves the White House after resigning

title: Woodstock
subtitle: “3 Days of Peace and Music” that came to define a generation
summary: In August 1969 nearly half a million young people gathered on Yasgur’s farm near Bethel, New York, for a music festival billed as “An Aquarian Exposition: 3 Days of Peace and Music.” Rain, mud, and shortages turned the weekend into an improvised city, and, for many, a demonstration of the counterculture’s ideals of peace and cooperation. Coming weeks after the Moon landing and amid conflict over the Vietnam War, civil rights, and sexual politics, Woodstock became shorthand for the youth culture of the 1960s.
thumbAlt: Festival-goers with a blanket tent in the crowd at Woodstock, 1969

title: The Wounded Knee Massacre
subtitle: The U.S. Army kills hundreds of Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek, December 1890
summary: On December 29, 1890, soldiers of the U.S. 7th Cavalry surrounded a band of Lakota led by Spotted Elk (Big Foot) at Wounded Knee Creek on the Pine Ridge Reservation and attempted to disarm them. A shot was fired, and the soldiers opened fire with heavy weapons, killing between 150 and 300 Lakota men, women, and children. About two dozen soldiers also died, many probably from their own side’s fire. Wounded Knee marked the end of sustained armed Native resistance on the Plains.
location: Wounded Knee Creek, Pine Ridge Reservation, South Dakota
thumbAlt: The aftermath of the Wounded Knee massacre

title: The Wright Brothers’ First Flight
subtitle: Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, December 17, 1903: the first powered, controlled airplane flights
summary: On the morning of December 17, 1903, on the windswept dunes of North Carolina’s Outer Banks, the Wright brothers’ engine-powered Wright Flyer stayed aloft for twelve seconds, the first powered, controlled flight of a heavier-than-air machine carrying a person. That day Wilbur and Orville made four flights; the longest lasted 59 seconds. Two bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, with no formal engineering training, they succeeded because they treated flight as a scientific problem to be solved step by step.
location: Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina
thumbAlt: John T. Daniels’s photograph of the Wright Flyer’s first flight on December 17, 1903, with Wilbur Wright running alongside the wingtip

title: Congress
subtitle: The legislative branch: the Senate and the House of Representatives
summary: Article I of the Constitution vests “All legislative Powers” in a Congress made up of a Senate and a House of Representatives. Members of the House are elected every two years, with seats apportioned by population; each state has two senators serving six-year terms. Congress makes the laws, levies taxes, declares war, confirms presidential appointments, and can impeach and remove officials. As the branch closest to the people, it has been the stage for many of the great debates of American history.
thumbAlt: The west front of the United States Capitol

title: The Continental Congress
subtitle: The colonies’ revolutionary assembly, and the first national government
summary: The Continental Congress began as a meeting of colonial delegates coordinating protest against British policy and became, almost by accident, the government of a new nation. The First Continental Congress (1774) organized a boycott of British goods; the Second (1775–1781) created the Continental Army, adopted the Declaration of Independence, conducted diplomacy, and drafted the Articles of Confederation.
location: Philadelphia (and, when the British threatened, Baltimore, Lancaster, York, and other towns)
thumbAlt: Engraving of the First Continental Congress in session

title: The Freedmen’s Bureau
subtitle: The federal agency that aided formerly enslaved people, 1865–1872
summary: Officially the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, the Freedmen’s Bureau was created by Congress in March 1865 to help formerly enslaved people make the transition to freedom. Led by General Oliver O. Howard, it issued food and clothing, ran hospitals, supervised labor contracts, helped found schools, legalized marriages made in slavery, and helped families reunite. Underfunded and opposed by President Andrew Johnson and white Southerners, it did most of its work between 1865 and 1868 and closed in 1872.
location: Headquarters in Washington, D.C.; offices throughout the South
thumbAlt: Alfred Waud’s drawing “The Freedmen’s Bureau”

title: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy
subtitle: The League of the Iroquois, a union of nations governed by the Great Law of Peace
summary: The Haudenosaunee (“People of the Longhouse”) are a confederacy of Native nations whose homelands lie mostly in present-day New York. According to their tradition, a prophet called the Peacemaker, with the help of Aionwatha (Hiawatha), persuaded five warring nations (the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca) to accept the Great Law of Peace. The Tuscarora later joined as a sixth nation. The Confederacy still exists, making it one of the longest-lasting participatory governments in the world.
location: Present-day New York State and neighboring regions; today also Ontario and Quebec
thumbAlt: Six Nations chiefs at Brantford explaining their wampum belts in 1871

title: Political Parties
subtitle: From Federalists and Republicans to the modern two-party system
summary: Political parties are not mentioned in the Constitution, and many founders hoped to avoid them. But parties formed almost immediately and have organized American politics ever since. The Federalists and Jefferson’s Democratic-Republicans gave way to Jacksonian Democrats and Whigs, and in the 1850s the antislavery Republican Party was born. Since then Democrats and Republicans have dominated a two-party system, even as their coalitions and ideas have shifted dramatically.
thumbAlt: Chart of the evolution of American political parties

title: The Presidency
subtitle: The executive branch and the office of president
summary: Article II of the Constitution vests “the executive Power” in a president, elected for a four-year term. The president is head of state, leader of the executive branch, and commander in chief of the armed forces, and must “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.” From George Washington’s precedents to Franklin D. Roosevelt’s transformation of the office, the presidency has grown into the most powerful position in American government, checked by Congress, the courts, and the voters.
thumbAlt: The north and south sides of the White House

title: The Supreme Court
subtitle: The highest court in the United States and the final interpreter of federal law
summary: The Supreme Court is the highest tribunal in the United States for all cases arising under the Constitution and federal law. The Constitution created it but said little about how it would work; Congress, and the justices themselves through their decisions, built the federal judiciary over time. From a weak body whose first justices complained about its lack of stature, it became, beginning with Chief Justice John Marshall, a co-equal branch that can strike down laws as unconstitutional.
location: Washington, D.C. (first met in New York City)
thumbAlt: The U.S. Supreme Court Building at dusk

title: United Nations
subtitle: The international organization founded in 1945 to keep the peace
summary: The United Nations was founded in 1945 by the victorious Allies of World War II to prevent future wars through collective security and international cooperation. Unlike the League of Nations after World War I, it had strong American backing: the Senate approved the UN Charter 89 to 2. The United States is one of five permanent members of the Security Council, each holding a veto. The UN has been a central, and often contested, arena of American foreign policy ever since.
thumbAlt: The United Nations General Assembly hall

title: Abolitionism
subtitle: The movement to end slavery in the United States
summary: Abolitionism was the movement to end slavery in the United States. Early antislavery reformers, many of them Quakers, worked for gradual emancipation and an end to the slave trade. In the 1830s a new generation, led by Black activists and white evangelicals such as William Lloyd Garrison, demanded immediate, uncompensated emancipation and equal rights for Black Americans. A small and often hated minority, abolitionists used newspapers, lectures, petitions, and the Underground Railroad to make slavery the central moral question of American politics. Their cause triumphed only through the Civil War and the Thirteenth Amendment.
thumbAlt: Frontispiece of the abolitionist book A Tribute for the Negro

title: Red Power and the American Indian Movement
subtitle: Native activism for sovereignty and self-determination, 1960s–1970s
summary: Inspired by the civil rights movement, young Native Americans in the 1960s and 1970s launched an intertribal movement known as Red Power to protest discrimination and assert tribal sovereignty. Activists held “fish-ins” to defend treaty fishing rights, occupied Alcatraz Island for nineteen months in 1969–1971, and, led by the American Indian Movement (AIM), occupied the town of Wounded Knee, South Dakota, for months in 1973. The movement helped end the federal policy of terminating tribes and win a policy of Indian self-determination.
location: Nationwide, including Alcatraz Island, Washington, D.C., the Pacific Northwest, and Wounded Knee, South Dakota
thumbAlt: Flag of Indians of All Tribes, the group that occupied Alcatraz

title: The Civil Rights Movement
subtitle: The mass struggle against segregation and disfranchisement, 1950s–1960s
summary: The civil rights movement was a mass campaign by Black Americans and their allies to end legal segregation and win the right to vote in the South. Building on decades of NAACP lawsuits, it won the Supreme Court’s Brown v. Board of Education decision in 1954 and then turned to nonviolent direct action: the Montgomery bus boycott, the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, the Birmingham campaign, the March on Washington, Freedom Summer, and the Selma marches. Its victories, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, dismantled Jim Crow in law and transformed American democracy.
thumbAlt: Civil rights demonstrators at a segregated public beach in Fort Lauderdale

title: The Environmental Movement
subtitle: From Silent Spring to Earth Day and the EPA
summary: In the 1960s, growing alarm about pollution, pesticides, and the destruction of open space produced a mass environmental movement. Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (1962) warned of the dangers of pesticides to wildlife and people. The first Earth Day, April 22, 1970, was, in the words of the American Yawp, the largest demonstration in history. A burst of lawmaking followed: the National Environmental Policy Act, the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970, and new laws to protect air, water, and endangered species.
thumbAlt: The whole Earth photographed from space by the Apollo 17 crew

title: The Farm Workers Movement
subtitle: The Delano grape strike, the boycott, and the United Farm Workers
summary: In the 1960s, Mexican American and Filipino farm workers in California organized to win union recognition, decent wages, and safe conditions. Their Delano grape strike, begun in 1965, and a nationwide consumer boycott of table grapes led by Cesar Chavez, Dolores Huerta, and Larry Itliong won the first major union contracts in California agriculture by 1970. The United Farm Workers became both a union and a civil rights movement.
location: California’s Central Valley and boycott centers nationwide
thumbAlt: Farm workers on strike in Delano, California, October 1965

title: The First Great Awakening
subtitle: A wave of evangelical revivals across the colonies, 1730s–1770s
summary: The First Great Awakening was a surge of evangelical Protestant revival that swept the American colonies from the 1730s to the 1770s, part of a movement also stirring Britain and Germany. Fiery preachers such as Jonathan Edwards and the traveling English evangelist George Whitefield urged listeners to experience a heartfelt conversion. The revivals split churches, challenged the authority of established clergy, and gave many colonists, including women and African Americans, new religious voices.
thumbAlt: Illustration of a religious camp meeting

title: The Great Migration
subtitle: Millions of Black Southerners move North and West, 1910s–1970
summary: Beginning around 1910 and continuing for half a century, millions of Black Southerners left the rural South for cities in the North, Midwest, and West, escaping Jim Crow, lynching, and poverty and seeking industrial jobs. Nearly half a million moved between 1910 and 1920 alone, spurred by wartime labor shortages, and about 1.5 million in the 1940s. The migration transformed American cities, politics, and culture, from Chicago and Detroit to Harlem, and laid foundations for the civil rights movement.
thumbAlt: Map of Black urban population changes during the Great Migration

title: The Harlem Renaissance
subtitle: A flowering of Black literature, art, and music in 1920s New York
summary: In the 1920s Harlem, in upper Manhattan, became what James Weldon Johnson called “the Culture Capital”. Writers such as Langston Hughes, Claude McKay, Jessie Redmon Fauset, and Zora Neale Hurston, along with artists, actors, and jazz musicians, produced a burst of creative work that came to be called the Harlem Renaissance or the New Negro Movement. Its leading figure Alain Locke declared that a new generation was achieving “something like a spiritual emancipation.”
thumbAlt: Portrait of the poet Langston Hughes, photographed by Carl Van Vechten in 1936

title: The Labor Movement
subtitle: Workers organize for wages, hours, and a voice on the job
summary: As industrial capitalism remade the United States after the Civil War, millions of wage workers, many of them immigrants, organized to win higher pay, shorter hours, safer conditions, and a say over their work. For half a century their biggest strikes were crushed. The Great Railroad Strike of 1877, the eight-hour campaign that ended at Haymarket, the Homestead strike, and the Pullman boycott were all broken by police, militias, private guards, court injunctions, or federal troops. Workers built new organizations anyway: the Knights of Labor, the American Federation of Labor, the Industrial Workers of the World, and garment unions built by young immigrant women. Only in 1935 did the Wagner Act guarantee most private-sector workers the right to organize and bargain collectively. Union membership then surged.
thumbAlt: Strikers at the start of the 1912 Lawrence textile strike

title: Populism and the People’s Party
subtitle: The farmers’ revolt of the 1890s
summary: Populism was a mass political movement of farmers in the South and West who believed that railroads, banks, and the two major parties served “the moneyed power” at the expense of ordinary producers. Organized first through the Farmers’ Alliance, they formed the People’s Party, which won congressional seats in 1890 and issued the sweeping Omaha Platform in 1892. In 1896 the Populists endorsed the Democrat William Jennings Bryan and soon faded, but many of their proposals later became law.
thumbAlt: Judge magazine cartoon of William Jennings Bryan in 1896

title: Progressivism
subtitle: Reformers confront the problems of industrial America, c. 1890s–1920
summary: Progressivism was not one movement but many. In the decades around 1900, reformers of every kind set out to fix the problems of industrial America: monopolies, corrupt political machines, dangerous workplaces, child labor, and city slums. Journalists exposed abuses, settlement workers moved into poor neighborhoods, ministers preached a social gospel, and women’s clubs, unions, and suffragists organized. Under Theodore Roosevelt, William Howard Taft, and Woodrow Wilson, the federal government took on new powers to regulate business. Four constitutional amendments followed between 1913 and 1920. Progressivism also had a darker side. In the South, white reformers presented disfranchisement and segregation as progressive measures, and many reformers shared the racial and anti-immigrant prejudices of their time.
thumbAlt: Jacob Riis’s photograph of Bandits’ Roost, an alley on Mulberry Street in New York

title: Second-Wave Feminism
subtitle: The women’s liberation movement of the 1960s and 1970s
summary: In the 1960s and 1970s, a new wave of feminism challenged discrimination against women in work, law, education, and family life. Inspired by the civil rights movement, and galvanized by Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963), activists founded the National Organization for Women, formed consciousness-raising groups, and fought for equal pay, reproductive rights, and an Equal Rights Amendment. They won major legal changes, including Roe v. Wade (1973), but the ERA was defeated by a conservative countermovement.
thumbAlt: President Kennedy signing the Equal Pay Act with members of the American Association of University Women

title: The Underground Railroad
subtitle: The secret network of freedom seekers and those who helped them escape slavery
summary: The Underground Railroad was not a railroad and not underground. It was the name for the efforts of enslaved African Americans to free themselves by escaping, and for the networks of people (free and enslaved Black Americans, white abolitionists, American Indians, and others) who helped them. Freedom seekers fled to the North, Canada, Mexico, Spanish Florida, the West, the Caribbean, and beyond, often guided by “conductors” such as Harriet Tubman. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, helping them became a federal crime, and the networks grew more organized and defiant.
thumbAlt: Charles T. Webber’s 1893 painting The Underground Railroad, showing freedom seekers arriving by wagon at a farmhouse in winter

title: The Woman Suffrage Movement
subtitle: Seventy-two years of struggle for women’s right to vote, 1848–1920
summary: The woman suffrage movement was the long campaign to win American women the right to vote. It began at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848 and ended in victory with the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920. Over seventy-two years, generations of women and some men lectured, petitioned, marched, lobbied, went to court, picketed the White House, and went to jail. The movement split over the Fifteenth Amendment, reunited in 1890, won state victories first in the West, and finally gained a federal amendment during World War I. Many of its white leaders sidelined Black women. Ida B. Wells and others fought for a movement that included them, and many women of color could not vote for decades after 1920.
thumbAlt: Illustration of suffrage activism in New York City

title: Abigail Adams
subtitle: Political partner, letter writer, and early voice for women’s rights
summary: Abigail Adams was the wife of the second president, John Adams, the mother of the sixth, John Quincy Adams, and one of the sharpest political minds of the Revolutionary generation. Through a lifetime of letters she advised her husband, reported on the war, ran the family farm and finances alone for years, and asked the men writing the nation’s new laws to “remember the ladies.” An early champion of women’s education and property rights, she was also an outspoken, politically engaged First Lady.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Abigail Adams

title: Abraham Lincoln
subtitle: Sixteenth president, who preserved the Union and ended slavery
summary: Abraham Lincoln rose from a one-room log cabin on the Kentucky frontier to become the sixteenth president of the United States. Elected in 1860 as the first Republican president, he led the Union through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, and pushed the Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery through Congress. He was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth in April 1865, days after the war’s end. Historians and the public alike rank him as the nation’s greatest president.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Abraham Lincoln

title: Alexander Hamilton
subtitle: First secretary of the Treasury and architect of the federal financial system
summary: Alexander Hamilton was born in the British West Indies, came to the mainland colonies as a teenager, and became one of the most influential of the nation’s founders. He served as George Washington’s aide during the Revolution, helped call the Constitutional Convention, and wrote most of the Federalist Papers in support of the Constitution. As the first secretary of the Treasury, from 1789 to 1795, he paid the Revolutionary War debts in full, had the federal government take over the states’ debts, and created the First Bank of the United States. His program and his preference for Britain divided the government and helped create the first political parties. He was killed in a duel with Vice President Aaron Burr in 1804.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Alexander Hamilton by John Trumbull

title: Amelia Earhart
subtitle: The first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, who vanished over the Pacific in 1937
summary: Amelia Earhart was one of the most influential pioneers of American aviation. In 1928 she became the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air, as a passenger, and in 1932 she flew it alone, five years to the day after Charles Lindbergh. She set record after record, including the first solo flight from Hawaiʻi to California, and used her fame to argue that women could do any job that men could. On July 2, 1937, nearing the end of an attempt to fly around the world, she and her navigator, Fred Noonan, vanished near tiny Howland Island in the Pacific. No trace of them was ever found.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Amelia Earhart in 1935

title: Andrew Carnegie
subtitle: Steel magnate and philanthropist of the Gilded Age
summary: Andrew Carnegie arrived in Pennsylvania as a poor thirteen-year-old Scottish immigrant and built the largest and most profitable steel company in the world. In 1901 he sold it to J. P. Morgan, who used it to create U.S. Steel, and Carnegie spent the rest of his life giving his fortune away, funding thousands of public libraries and institutions. His mills were also the scene of the violent 1892 Homestead strike, and he remains a symbol of both the opportunity and the inequality of the Gilded Age.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Andrew Carnegie

title: Andrew Jackson
subtitle: Seventh president, champion of the “common man,” and architect of Indian removal
summary: Andrew Jackson was the dominant figure in American politics between Thomas Jefferson and Abraham Lincoln. He was the first president from the West and the first “self-made man” to reach the White House. Orphaned by the Revolution, he rose as a Tennessee lawyer, planter, and enslaver, and his victory at New Orleans in 1815 made him a national hero. As president from 1829 to 1837 he cast himself as the people’s champion against privilege, destroyed the Second Bank of the United States, faced down South Carolina’s nullification of federal law, and founded the Democratic Party. He also signed the Indian Removal Act, which drove the Native nations of the Southeast from their homelands and led to the Cherokee Trail of Tears.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Andrew Jackson

title: Babe Ruth
subtitle: The slugger who transformed baseball and became the most celebrated athlete of the 1920s
summary: Babe Ruth was a troubled Baltimore boy raised in a reform school who became the most celebrated athlete of his time. A star pitcher for the Boston Red Sox, he was sold to the New York Yankees in 1920 and turned the home run from a rarity into the heart of the game, hitting 54 that year, more than all but one other major league team, and 60 in 1927. Larger than life on and off the field, he embodied the boisterous 1920s, filled ballparks across the country, and retired with 714 home runs.
thumbAlt: Babe Ruth in his first year with the New York Yankees, 1920

title: Barack Obama
subtitle: Forty-fourth president and the first African American president
summary: Barack Obama was inaugurated on January 20, 2009, as the forty-fourth president and the first African American to hold the office. The son of a white mother from Kansas and a Black Kenyan father, he grew up in Hawaii and Indonesia, worked as a community organizer in Chicago, and led the Harvard Law Review before entering politics. He took office in a deep recession, won an $800 billion stimulus, and signed the Affordable Care Act, which sharply reduced the number of uninsured Americans. Abroad he withdrew most American troops from Iraq, ordered the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, and pursued agreements on Iran’s nuclear program and climate change. Republican control of Congress after 2010 blocked much of his later agenda.
thumbAlt: Official portrait of Barack Obama

title: Benjamin Franklin
subtitle: Printer, scientist, diplomat, and the Revolution’s elder statesman
summary: Benjamin Franklin rose from a Boston candlemaker’s son to become the best-known American of the eighteenth century, as a printer, writer, scientist, and statesman. In Philadelphia he published Poor Richard’s Almanack and founded a library, a fire company, a hospital, and the academy that became the University of Pennsylvania. His experiments with electricity won him international fame. He represented the colonies in London for nearly two decades, helped draft the Declaration of Independence, won the French alliance, and helped negotiate the peace with Britain. At eighty-one he was the oldest delegate to the Constitutional Convention. An enslaver earlier in life, he ended it as president of an abolition society.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Benjamin Franklin by Joseph Siffred Duplessis

title: Booker T. Washington
subtitle: Educator and the most influential Black leader of his generation
summary: Booker T. Washington was born into slavery in Virginia and became the most prominent Black educator and spokesman of his time. As the founding principal of Alabama’s Tuskegee Institute, he championed industrial and vocational education as the road to Black economic independence. His 1895 Atlanta Exposition address, which seemed to accept segregation in exchange for economic opportunity, made him famous and drew sharp criticism from W. E. B. Du Bois, who called it the “Atlanta Compromise.” In 1901 he became the first African American invited to dine at the White House.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Booker T. Washington

title: Cesar Chavez
subtitle: Labor leader and co-founder of the United Farm Workers
summary: Cesar Chavez was the Mexican American labor leader who, with Dolores Huerta, built the first lasting union of farmworkers in the United States. The son of migrant laborers who had lost their Arizona farm, he founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962, joined the great Delano grape strike of 1965, and turned it into a national boycott of table grapes. Through strikes, marches, and long public fasts, always insisting on nonviolence, he made the United Farm Workers a union and a civil rights movement at once, and became the best-known figure of the Chicano movement.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Cesar Chavez

title: Donald Trump
subtitle: Forty-fifth and forty-seventh president, the second ever elected to non-consecutive terms
summary: Donald Trump, a New York real estate developer and reality-television star, won the presidency in 2016 as a Republican in a surprise victory, without ever having held public office or military command. His first term brought a large tax cut, tighter immigration policies, new tariffs, and an “America First” foreign policy, along with intense partisan division and two impeachments, both ending in acquittal. He lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden, refused to concede, and his supporters attacked the Capitol on January 6, 2021. In 2024, after being convicted on state felony charges in New York, he won the presidency again, becoming only the second president elected to non-consecutive terms.
thumbAlt: Official White House portrait of President Donald Trump, 2017

title: Dwight D. Eisenhower
subtitle: Commander of the D-Day invasion and thirty-fourth president, who presided over the prosperous, anxious 1950s
summary: Dwight D. Eisenhower rose in five years from an obscure lieutenant colonel to Supreme Commander of the Allied invasion of Nazi-occupied Europe on D-Day. Elected president in 1952 and 1956, “Ike” ended the Korean War, built the Interstate Highway System, and kept the country out of new wars while waging the Cold War with nuclear deterrence and CIA covert action. He sent troops to enforce school desegregation in Little Rock but never endorsed the Brown decision, and on leaving office he warned Americans against the “military-industrial complex.”
thumbAlt: Official portrait photograph of President Dwight D. Eisenhower, 1959

title: Eleanor Roosevelt
subtitle: First lady, reformer, and champion of human rights
summary: Eleanor Roosevelt transformed the role of First Lady and became, in the words later used of her, the “First Lady of the World.” An orphaned girl from a wealthy family, she grew into a political force in her own right: during Franklin D. Roosevelt’s presidency she traveled the country as his “eyes, ears and legs,” pressed the New Deal to include women and Black Americans, and wrote a daily newspaper column. After his death she represented the United States at the United Nations, where she chaired the Human Rights Commission and helped write the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Eleanor Roosevelt

title: Elizabeth Cady Stanton
subtitle: Philosopher and strategist of the women’s rights movement
summary: Elizabeth Cady Stanton was the chief philosopher of the American women’s rights movement. In 1848 she helped organize the Seneca Falls Convention and wrote its Declaration of Sentiments, which rewrote the Declaration of Independence to proclaim that “all men and women are created equal.” For half a century she supplied the ideas, and her partner Susan B. Anthony carried them across the country. A radical on marriage, divorce, and religion, she also opposed voting rights for Black men without women, a stance that split the suffrage movement.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Elizabeth Cady Stanton

title: Elvis Presley
subtitle: The “King of Rock & Roll,” who carried a blend of Black and white Southern music to a mass audience
summary: Elvis Presley, a young truck driver from Tupelo, Mississippi, began recording at a Memphis studio in the early 1950s and, in 1954, set off a musical and cultural revolution. Mixing blues, rhythm and blues, country, and gospel, he brought music rooted in Black traditions to huge white audiences, and his hip-shaking performances shocked parents as much as they thrilled teenagers. After a string of number-one hits, national television appearances, and movies, he served in the Army, spent the 1960s making films, and returned to the stage in 1969. He died at his Memphis home, Graceland, in 1977, at forty-two.
thumbAlt: Publicity photograph of Elvis Presley for the 1957 film Jailhouse Rock

title: Franklin D. Roosevelt
subtitle: Thirty-second president, architect of the New Deal and wartime leader
summary: Franklin D. Roosevelt led the United States through the two great crises of the twentieth century, the Great Depression and World War II, and was the only president elected four times. Born to wealth and paralyzed by polio at thirty-nine, he returned to politics and won the presidency in 1932 by promising “a new deal for the American people.” His New Deal transformed the federal government’s role in American life. As commander in chief after Pearl Harbor, he built the alliance with Britain, the Soviet Union, and China that defeated Germany and Japan. He died in April 1945, weeks before victory in Europe.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Franklin D. Roosevelt

title: Frederick Douglass
subtitle: Escaped slave, orator, editor, and the foremost Black leader of the nineteenth century
summary: Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the most important leader of the movement for African American civil rights in the nineteenth century. His Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845) became a bestseller, and his speeches, above all “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” (1852), made him the nation’s most famous abolitionist orator. He edited his own newspaper, supported women’s rights from the Seneca Falls Convention onward, recruited Black soldiers during the Civil War, and pressed Abraham Lincoln face to face for equal treatment. After the war he held federal office under five presidents.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Frederick Douglass

title: George Washington
subtitle: Commander of the Continental Army and first president
summary: George Washington commanded the Continental Army through eight years of war, presided over the convention that wrote the Constitution, and served as the first president of the United States. Twice he gave up power when he could have kept it, by resigning his command in 1783 and by retiring after two terms as president, and those choices, more than any battle, made him the “indispensable man” of the founding. A Virginia planter who held hundreds of people in slavery, he arranged in his will to free those he owned, but only after his wife’s death.
thumbAlt: Portrait of George Washington by Gilbert Stuart

title: Harriet Tubman
subtitle: Freedom seeker, Underground Railroad conductor, Union scout
summary: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery on Maryland’s Eastern Shore around 1822, escaped in 1849, and then went back again and again to lead family members and friends to freedom, becoming the most famous conductor of the Underground Railroad. During the Civil War she served the Union Army as a nurse, scout, and spy, and in June 1863 she helped plan and lead the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, which freed more than 700 enslaved people. In her later years in Auburn, New York, she supported women’s suffrage and opened a home for elderly and poor African Americans.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Harriet Tubman seated

title: Harry S. Truman
subtitle: Thirty-third president: ended World War II and launched the Cold War containment policy
summary: Harry S. Truman, the thirty-third president of the United States (1945–1953), was a Missouri farmer, artillery captain, and failed shopkeeper who became president when Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945, after just eighty-two days as vice president. Within months he approved the atomic bombing of Japan; over the next seven years he shaped America’s response to the Soviet Union with the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan and NATO, desegregated the armed forces, and led the country into the Korean War. He left office deeply unpopular, but historians now rank him among the best presidents.
thumbAlt: Official portrait photograph of Harry S. Truman

title: Henry Ford
subtitle: Automaker who put America on wheels with the Model T, the moving assembly line, and the Five Dollar Day
summary: Henry Ford did not invent the automobile or the assembly line, but more than anyone else he turned the car from a rich man’s novelty into a machine for the multitude. His Model T of 1908 was cheap, rugged, and easy to fix; his moving assembly line of 1913 cut its assembly time dramatically; and his Five Dollar Day of 1914 doubled workers’ pay so that they could buy the cars they built. Ford became a folk hero, and also one of the most notorious antisemites in American history, whose newspaper spread conspiracy theories that the Nazis admired.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Henry Ford, about 1919

title: Ida B. Wells
subtitle: Journalist who exposed lynching and fought for civil rights and suffrage
summary: Ida B. Wells was born into slavery in Mississippi in 1862 and became the leading crusader against lynching in American history. After a Memphis mob lynched three Black grocers, one of them her close friend, in 1892, she investigated lynchings across the South. In Southern Horrors and A Red Record she exposed the charge of rape used to justify them as a myth. A white mob destroyed her newspaper, and she carried her campaign to the North and to Britain. In Chicago she helped found Black women’s clubs, helped organize the NAACP, and fought for women’s suffrage. In 2020 she was awarded a posthumous Pulitzer Prize.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Ida B. Wells

title: Jackie Robinson
subtitle: The ballplayer who broke baseball’s color barrier in 1947, and a civil rights advocate
summary: On April 15, 1947, Jackie Robinson took the field for the Brooklyn Dodgers and became the first African American player in the twentieth century in the American or National League. Chosen by Dodgers executive Branch Rickey, he endured hostile crowds, opposed teammates, and threats while starring on the field: Rookie of the Year in 1947, Most Valuable Player in 1949, and six pennants in ten seasons. After retiring he became an outspoken advocate for civil rights.
thumbAlt: Jackie Robinson in the uniform of the Kansas City Monarchs

title: James Madison
subtitle: Architect of the Constitution and fourth president
summary: James Madison, a Virginia planter and enslaver, did more than anyone to design the Constitution of the United States. His exertions earned him the title “Father of the Constitution,” though he insisted the document was the work of “many heads & many hands.” He drafted the Virginia Plan that framed the Convention’s debates, wrote twenty-nine of the Federalist Papers, and steered the Bill of Rights through the first Congress. With Thomas Jefferson he founded the Republican Party, which opposed Hamilton’s Federalists. As Jefferson’s secretary of state and then as president from 1809 to 1817, he led the country through the troubled years before and during the War of 1812.
thumbAlt: Portrait of James Madison

title: Joe Biden
subtitle: Forty-sixth president, after thirty-six years in the Senate and eight as vice president
summary: Joe Biden, a working-class Catholic from Scranton who overcame a severe childhood stutter, was elected to the Senate at twenty-nine, weeks before a car crash killed his wife and baby daughter. He served thirty-six years in the Senate and eight as Barack Obama’s vice president, then defeated Donald Trump in 2020 to become, at seventy-eight, the oldest president inaugurated up to that time. He led the country through the end of the Covid-19 pandemic and signed major laws on economic relief, infrastructure, semiconductors, and clean energy, but faced high inflation, a chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan, and doubts about his age, and he withdrew from the 2024 race.
thumbAlt: Official portrait of President Joe Biden, 2021

title: John Adams
subtitle: Revolutionary leader, diplomat, and second president, who kept the young nation out of war with France
summary: John Adams was a blunt, brilliant Massachusetts lawyer who became one of the leading voices for American independence, a diplomat who helped negotiate the peace with Britain, the nation’s first vice president, and its second president. As president he faced a near-war with Revolutionary France; he built up the navy but chose peace, an achievement he called the great jewel of his career. He also signed the notorious Alien and Sedition Acts, and he lost the bitter election of 1800 to his rival and friend Thomas Jefferson.
thumbAlt: Portrait of John Adams by Gilbert Stuart

title: John Brown
subtitle: Abolitionist who led the 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry
summary: John Brown was a white abolitionist who believed slavery was a sin that only violence could end. After killing pro-slavery settlers in “Bleeding Kansas,” he led twenty-one men in an attack on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, in October 1859, hoping to spark an uprising of enslaved people. The raid collapsed within thirty-six hours; Brown was captured, tried for treason, and hanged. Hailed as a martyr in the North and denounced as a terrorist in the South, he deepened the division that led to the Civil War.
thumbAlt: Daguerreotype of John Brown with his hand raised

title: John F. Kennedy
subtitle: Thirty-fifth president: the youngest ever elected, assassinated in Dallas in 1963
summary: John F. Kennedy was the youngest person ever elected president and the first Roman Catholic to hold the office. A rich Bostonian who became a war hero in the Pacific, he beat Richard Nixon in 1960 in one of the closest elections in American history, helped by a series of televised debates. In less than three years he faced the Bay of Pigs fiasco, the building of the Berlin Wall, and the Cuban Missile Crisis, launched the race to the moon, and sent a civil rights bill to Congress. His assassination in Dallas on November 22, 1963, became one of the great national traumas.
thumbAlt: Official White House portrait photograph of President John F. Kennedy, July 1963

title: John Marshall
subtitle: Fourth Chief Justice, who made the Supreme Court a co-equal branch
summary: John Marshall was the fourth Chief Justice of the United States and the longest-serving, presiding over the Supreme Court for thirty-four years, from 1801 to 1835. A Revolutionary War officer and Virginia lawyer, he took over a weak, little-respected tribunal and made it a co-equal branch of government. In Marbury v. Madison he established the Court’s power to strike down unconstitutional laws; in McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden he gave the federal government broad power. More than any other judge, he defined what the Constitution would mean in practice.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Chief Justice John Marshall

title: Louis Armstrong
subtitle: New Orleans trumpeter and singer who made jazz a soloist’s art and a world music
summary: Louis Armstrong grew up poor in New Orleans, learned the cornet in a reform school, and followed his mentor Joe “King” Oliver to Chicago in 1922. His Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings of the 1920s put the improvising soloist at the center of jazz and popularized scat singing. Over a career of relentless touring, radio, and film, from “Heebie Jeebies” to “Hello, Dolly!” and “What a Wonderful World,” “Satchmo” became one of the most famous musicians in the world.
thumbAlt: Louis Armstrong holding his trumpet, smiling

title: Lyndon B. Johnson
subtitle: Thirty-sixth president: the Great Society, civil rights, and Vietnam
summary: Lyndon Baines Johnson, the thirty-sixth president of the United States (1963–1969), was a Texas Hill Country schoolteacher who became one of the most skilled legislators in American history. Thrust into the presidency by John F. Kennedy’s assassination in November 1963, he pushed through the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, won a historic landslide, and launched the Great Society: Medicare, Medicaid, federal aid to education, and the War on Poverty. But his escalation of the Vietnam War tore the country apart, and in 1968 he declined to seek another term.
thumbAlt: Official portrait photograph of Lyndon B. Johnson

title: Malcolm X
subtitle: Black nationalist leader and critic of nonviolence
summary: Malcolm X was the most visible voice of Black nationalism in the 1960s. Born Malcolm Little, he rose from a shattered childhood and a prison cell to become the national spokesman of the Nation of Islam, denouncing white racism and rejecting Martin Luther King Jr.’s nonviolence; he urged Black Americans to seek freedom “by any means necessary.” In 1964 he broke with the Nation, made the pilgrimage to Mecca, and began building bridges to the civil rights movement. He was assassinated in February 1965; his ideas shaped the Black Power movement.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Malcolm X

title: Mark Twain
subtitle: Humorist and novelist who turned American speech into literature
summary: Samuel Clemens grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi River, worked as a printer, riverboat pilot, and frontier journalist, and as “Mark Twain” became the best-loved American writer of his age. Books such as The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn drew on his Missouri boyhood, while The Gilded Age and later works attacked corruption, greed, racism, and imperialism. In his time he was considered the funniest man on earth.
thumbAlt: Mark Twain in a white suit, photographed in his later years

title: Martin Luther King Jr.
subtitle: Minister and leader of the nonviolent civil rights movement
summary: Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist minister from Atlanta, became the most prominent leader of the civil rights movement. Chosen to lead the Montgomery bus boycott soon after he arrived in the city as a young pastor, he joined the ideals of Christianity to Gandhi’s methods of nonviolent resistance. He led campaigns in Birmingham and Selma, delivered “I Have a Dream” at the March on Washington, and helped win the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act. At thirty-five he became the youngest man to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968, while supporting a strike of sanitation workers.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Martin Luther King Jr.

title: Muhammad Ali
subtitle: Three-time heavyweight champion who gave up his title rather than fight in Vietnam
summary: Muhammad Ali, born Cassius Clay in segregated Louisville, won Olympic gold at eighteen and the world heavyweight title at twenty-two. That year he announced that he had joined the Nation of Islam and taken a new name. In 1967 he refused induction into the Army during the Vietnam War, citing his faith; he was stripped of his title, convicted, and barred from boxing until the Supreme Court overturned his conviction in 1971. He regained the championship twice, and after Parkinson’s disease ended his public career he became a worldwide symbol of conviction and humanitarian work.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Muhammad Ali in 1967

title: Neil Armstrong
subtitle: Test pilot and astronaut who became the first person to walk on the Moon, on July 20, 1969
summary: Neil Armstrong was an Ohio-born engineer and test pilot who flew the X-15 rocket plane to the edge of space, saved his crew during NASA’s first life-threatening emergency in orbit, and on July 20, 1969, as commander of Apollo 11, became the first person to set foot on the Moon. An estimated 650 million people watched him step onto the lunar surface. He left NASA in 1971 to teach engineering.
thumbAlt: Official NASA portrait of Neil Armstrong in his spacesuit, 1969

title: Richard Nixon
subtitle: Thirty-seventh president: opened relations with China, then became the only president to resign
summary: Richard Nixon rose from a small California town to the vice presidency in six years, lost the presidency to John F. Kennedy in 1960, and won it in 1968. A lifelong anticommunist, he stunned the world by visiting Communist China in 1972, signed landmark nuclear arms limitation treaties with the Soviet Union, and ended the American ground war in Vietnam; at home he created the Environmental Protection Agency. Reelected in a 49-state landslide, he was brought down by the Watergate scandal and in 1974 became the first and only president to resign.
thumbAlt: Official presidential portrait photograph of Richard Nixon, 1972

title: Ronald Reagan
subtitle: Fortieth president and leader of the conservative revival
summary: Ronald Reagan, a former radio announcer, film actor, and governor of California, was elected president in 1980 at a time of economic trouble and setbacks abroad. He cut income taxes, broke an air traffic controllers’ strike, and built up the military as deficits and the national debt soared. After denouncing the Soviet Union, he worked with Mikhail Gorbachev on the 1987 INF Treaty, the first Cold War agreement to reduce nuclear arsenals. Despite the Iran-Contra affair, he left office in 1989 highly popular, having reshaped American conservatism.
thumbAlt: Official portrait of Ronald Reagan

title: Rosa Parks
subtitle: Activist whose arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott
summary: Rosa Parks was the seamstress and veteran NAACP activist whose arrest on December 1, 1955, for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger on a Montgomery, Alabama, bus sparked the Montgomery bus boycott. The thirteen-month protest ended with bus segregation struck down and made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader. Long remembered as a tired woman who simply wanted to sit down, Parks was in fact a seasoned organizer who had fought Jim Crow for more than a decade. “The only tired I was,” she wrote, “was tired of giving in.”
thumbAlt: Photograph of Rosa Parks

title: Sacagawea
subtitle: The Lemhi Shoshone teenager who traveled with Lewis and Clark’s Corps of Discovery
summary: Sacagawea was a Lemhi Shoshone woman who, at sixteen or seventeen and carrying her newborn son, traveled with the Lewis and Clark Expedition on its journey west and back. The only woman in the Corps of Discovery, she is often remembered as its guide, but the expedition’s journals show something different and arguably more important: her presence told the tribes they met that the party was not a war party, and when the explorers reached her homeland in the Rockies, she helped them find the Shoshone and the horses they needed to cross the mountains.
thumbAlt: Alice Cooper’s statue of Sacagawea at the 1905 Lewis and Clark Exposition in Portland, Oregon

title: Sitting Bull
subtitle: Hunkpapa Lakota leader who refused the reservation
summary: Sitting Bull (Tatanka-Iyotanka) was a Hunkpapa Lakota war chief and holy man who led the Lakota who refused to accept life on a reservation. He rejected the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie and kept his people hunting buffalo on the open plains. In June 1876 his vision of soldiers “falling into camp” came before the Lakota and Cheyenne victory over George Armstrong Custer at the Little Bighorn. Pursued by the army, he led his followers into Canada and surrendered in 1881. He toured briefly with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West and lived at Standing Rock. In December 1890, amid fears of the Ghost Dance, he was killed by Lakota reservation police sent to arrest him.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Sitting Bull

title: Sojourner Truth
subtitle: Abolitionist and women’s rights speaker who escaped slavery in New York
summary: Sojourner Truth was born into slavery in New York as Isabella Baumfree, freed herself in 1826, and became one of the most powerful speakers of the nineteenth century against slavery and for women’s rights. She was the first Black woman to win a lawsuit against a white man, for the return of her son, sold illegally into Alabama. Never formally educated, she dictated a celebrated autobiography and moved audiences with speeches such as the one at Akron in 1851 later known as “Ain’t I a Woman?” In 2009 she became the first Black woman honored with a bust in the U.S. Capitol.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Sojourner Truth

title: Susan B. Anthony
subtitle: Organizer and public face of the woman suffrage movement
summary: Susan B. Anthony was the best-known organizer of the nineteenth-century woman suffrage movement. For more than fifty years, often in partnership with Elizabeth Cady Stanton, she traveled the country giving speeches, circulating petitions, and building organizations. Raised a Quaker, she began as a temperance and antislavery reformer. After the Civil War she opposed the Fifteenth Amendment because it enfranchised Black men but not women, and she co-founded the National Woman Suffrage Association. In 1872 she was arrested and convicted for voting. She died in 1906. The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, was widely called the “Susan B. Anthony Amendment.”
thumbAlt: Photograph of Susan B. Anthony

title: Tecumseh
subtitle: Shawnee leader who built a confederacy of Native nations
summary: Tecumseh was a Shawnee leader who, with his brother Tenskwatawa, “the Prophet,” tried to unite the Native nations between the Great Lakes and the Gulf of Mexico against American expansion. He argued that Native lands belonged to all Native peoples in common and could not be sold by any single nation. His confederacy fought alongside Britain in the War of 1812, and his death at the Battle of the Thames in 1813 ended the last great effort at pan-Native resistance east of the Mississippi.
thumbAlt: Portrait of Tecumseh

title: Theodore Roosevelt
subtitle: Twenty-sixth president and champion of the “Square Deal”
summary: Theodore Roosevelt became president in 1901, at forty-two, after the assassination of William McKinley. He was the youngest person ever to hold the office. Historians often call him the first modern president, because he made the White House, rather than Congress or the parties, the center of American politics. His “Square Deal” used federal power to regulate big business, protect consumers, and conserve the nation’s forests and wild lands. Abroad he built up the Navy, secured the Panama Canal, and declared the United States the “policeman” of the Western Hemisphere. In 1912 he ran again as the candidate of his own Progressive Party.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Theodore Roosevelt

title: Thomas Edison
subtitle: Inventor of the phonograph and a practical electric light, and creator of the modern research laboratory
summary: Thomas Edison, a boy with only a few months of schooling who sold newspapers on a Michigan railroad, became one of the most celebrated inventors in American history. At his Menlo Park, New Jersey, laboratory, the first industrial research lab, he invented the phonograph in 1877 and developed a practical electric light and the whole system needed to power it; in 1882 his Pearl Street station began lighting lower Manhattan. Later, at West Orange, he helped create the recording and motion picture industries. To his countrymen he became a living symbol of American ingenuity.
thumbAlt: Portrait photograph of Thomas Edison, seated, around 1922

title: Thomas Jefferson
subtitle: Author of the Declaration of Independence and third president
summary: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, served as the first secretary of state and the third president, doubled the size of the nation with the Louisiana Purchase, and founded the University of Virginia. He was the leading voice of a republic of independent farmers, limited government, and religious freedom. He was also a lifelong slaveholder who owned more than 600 people over his lifetime, freed only a handful, and most likely fathered six children with Sally Hemings, an enslaved woman in his household. As Encyclopedia Virginia puts it, each generation has claimed him “on both sides of almost every important question.”
thumbAlt: Portrait of Thomas Jefferson by Rembrandt Peale

title: Thurgood Marshall
subtitle: Civil rights lawyer and first Black justice of the Supreme Court
summary: Thurgood Marshall was the lawyer who led the legal campaign against segregation and, in 1967, became the first African American justice of the Supreme Court. As chief counsel of the NAACP and director of its Legal Defense and Educational Fund, he won nearly thirty Supreme Court cases, above all Brown v. Board of Education (1954), which struck down school segregation. He then served as a federal appeals judge and as solicitor general before joining the Court, where until 1991 he was a forceful liberal voice for individual and civil rights.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Justice Thurgood Marshall

title: Ulysses S. Grant
subtitle: Union general who won the Civil War and eighteenth president
summary: Ulysses S. Grant was the Union general who won the Civil War and the eighteenth president of the United States (1869–1877). A quiet tanner’s son who failed at farming and business before the war, he rose in four years to command all Union armies, took Vicksburg, wore down Robert E. Lee’s army, and accepted its surrender at Appomattox. As president he fought for the Fifteenth Amendment and sent troops against the Ku Klux Klan, but scandals among his appointees long dominated his reputation, which historians are now reassessing.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Ulysses S. Grant

title: Walt Disney
subtitle: Creator of Mickey Mouse, the animated feature film, and Disneyland
summary: Walt Disney grew up on a Missouri farm and in Kansas City, went bankrupt with his first cartoon studio, and moved to Hollywood with almost nothing. With his brother Roy and the animator Ub Iwerks he created Mickey Mouse, who became a star in Steamboat Willie (1928), a cartoon with synchronized music that became the most successful sound cartoon of its day. His studio made Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), the first full-length animated feature, and later used television to build a new kind of entertainment empire, crowned by Disneyland in 1955. He won more Academy Awards than anyone in history.
thumbAlt: Walt Disney on the Place de la Concorde in Paris in 1935

title: W. E. B. Du Bois
subtitle: Scholar, editor, and co-founder of the NAACP
summary: W. E. B. Du Bois was the foremost Black intellectual of the early twentieth century and one of its most uncompromising voices for civil rights. The first African American to earn a PhD at Harvard, he pioneered the sociological study of Black life and wrote The Souls of Black Folk (1903), which challenged Booker T. Washington’s accommodation to segregation. He founded the Niagara Movement in 1905, helped found the NAACP in 1909, and for nearly a quarter century edited its magazine, The Crisis. He was also a leader of the Pan-African movement. He died in Ghana on the eve of the 1963 March on Washington.
thumbAlt: Photograph of W. E. B. Du Bois

title: Woodrow Wilson
subtitle: Twenty-eighth president: progressive reformer, wartime leader, and segregationist
summary: Woodrow Wilson, the twenty-eighth president of the United States (1913–1921), was a political scientist who rose within three years from president of Princeton University to the White House. His “New Freedom” reforms created the Federal Reserve and expanded federal regulation of business; he led the nation into World War I and proposed, in his Fourteen Points, a League of Nations to keep the peace. The Senate rejected his treaty, and a stroke left him incapacitated. His vision shaped American internationalism, but he also extended segregation in the federal government and suppressed wartime dissent.
thumbAlt: Photograph of Woodrow Wilson

title: Alcatraz Island
subtitle: San Francisco Bay island: a prison, then the site of the 1969–1971 Indian occupation
summary: Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay is best known as a former prison, but it is also a landmark of Native American activism. From November 1969 to June 1971, a group calling itself Indians of All Tribes occupied the island, demanding it for an Indian university and cultural center. Their nineteen-month occupation drew national attention to Native rights and helped change federal Indian policy. The island is now part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area.
location: San Francisco Bay, California (Golden Gate National Recreation Area)
thumbAlt: Alcatraz Island seen from the east

title: Angel Island Immigration Station
subtitle: The West Coast station built to enforce exclusion, 1910–1940
summary: The immigration station on Angel Island in San Francisco Bay opened in 1910. Unlike Ellis Island, it was designed to detain rather than welcome: under the Chinese Exclusion Act and later laws, Chinese and other Asian immigrants faced long detentions and grueling interrogations to prove their right to enter. Some waited weeks, others years. Detainees carved poems into the barracks walls that survive today.
thumbAlt: The detention barracks at the Angel Island Immigration Station

title: Cahokia
subtitle: The largest city in North America north of Mexico before 1492
summary: Around a thousand years ago, Cahokia, near the Mississippi River in present-day Illinois, was the greatest city north of Mexico. Estimates of its population at its height range from about 10,000 to 30,000, comparable to many cities of the time in Europe and the ancient Near East, and its builders raised more than a hundred earthen mounds around great plazas. Cahokia was the leading center of the Mississippian culture, which spread across the Mississippi Valley and the Southeast.
location: Collinsville, Illinois, east of St. Louis
thumbAlt: Earthen mounds at Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site

title: Little Rock Central High School
subtitle: Site of the 1957 desegregation crisis, now a National Historic Site
summary: Little Rock Central High School became a battleground in 1957, when nine Black students, the Little Rock Nine, needed federal troops to attend classes there. Built beginning in 1926, the school is still an operating public high school and is also a National Historic Site managed by the National Park Service, which offers guided tours of the grounds.
thumbAlt: Little Rock Central High School

title: Chaco Canyon
subtitle: Ceremonial center of the ancestral Pueblo world
summary: In a high, dry canyon in northwestern New Mexico, ancestral Pueblo people built a center unlike anything else in North America. Beginning in the mid-800s, they raised multistory stone “great houses” with hundreds of rooms, aligned buildings to the sun and moon, and linked Chaco by roads to more than 150 great houses across the region. By about 1050, Chaco was the ceremonial, administrative, and economic center of the San Juan Basin.
location: San Juan Basin, northwestern New Mexico
thumbAlt: The great kiva plaza at Chetro Ketl in Chaco Canyon

title: Ellis Island
subtitle: The nation’s busiest immigration station, 1892–1924
summary: From 1892 to 1924, Ellis Island in New York Harbor was America’s largest and busiest immigration station, where more than 12 million immigrants were processed. Most passed inspection in a few hours and went on to new lives; for some it was an “Island of Tears,” where families were separated and people were turned away. Today it is part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument and home to a museum of immigration.
thumbAlt: Ellis Island immigration station in 1902

title: Harpers Ferry
subtitle: Armory town where John Brown struck at slavery
summary: Harpers Ferry, at the meeting of the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers, was home to a U.S. armory where interchangeable parts were first successfully used in manufacturing. In October 1859 the abolitionist John Brown seized the armory in a failed attempt to spark a slave uprising. During the Civil War it saw the largest surrender of Union troops of the war. After the war it became home to one of the earliest integrated schools in the country.
location: Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, where the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers meet
thumbAlt: The armory engine house known as John Brown’s Fort at Harpers Ferry

title: Independence Hall
subtitle: Where the Declaration and the Constitution were debated and signed
summary: Built as the Pennsylvania State House, Independence Hall is where the Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence in 1776 and where the Constitutional Convention wrote the Constitution in 1787. Today it is part of Independence National Historical Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
thumbAlt: Independence Hall in Philadelphia

title: Manzanar
subtitle: A War Relocation Center in California’s Owens Valley, now a National Historic Site
summary: Manzanar was one of ten War Relocation Centers where Japanese Americans were incarcerated during World War II. Built in 1942 on land the Army leased from the city of Los Angeles in California’s Owens Valley, at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, it held families forcibly removed from the West Coast under Executive Order 9066. Today it is a National Historic Site that preserves the camp’s story, and the earlier displacement of the valley’s Paiute people and farm settlers.
location: Owens Valley, Inyo County, California (between Lone Pine and Independence on U.S. 395)
thumbAlt: People exercising at Manzanar with mountains behind

title: Mesa Verde
subtitle: Cliff dwellings of the Ancestral Pueblo people
summary: Mesa Verde, in southwestern Colorado, preserves some of the largest and best-preserved cliff dwellings in North America. Ancestral Pueblo people lived on the mesa tops for centuries, then, between about 1180 and 1300, built stone villages tucked into cliff alcoves. Within about a century they had migrated south to join communities in present-day New Mexico and Arizona, where their descendants live today.
thumbAlt: Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde

title: Mount Rushmore
subtitle: Four presidents carved into the Black Hills, on land sacred to the Lakota
summary: Between 1927 and 1941, sculptor Gutzon Borglum and about 400 workers blasted and carved the faces of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln into a granite mountain in South Dakota’s Black Hills. Meant to represent the nation’s birth, growth, development, and preservation, it draws more than two million visitors a year. But the Black Hills were recognized by treaty as Lakota land and are sacred to many tribes, and the memorial remains a contested symbol.
thumbAlt: The carved faces of Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Lincoln on Mount Rushmore

title: The National Mall
subtitle: “America’s Front Yard” in Washington, D.C.
summary: The National Mall is the great open space at the heart of Washington, D.C., stretching from the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River. Planned as part of Pierre L’Enfant’s design for the capital, commissioned by George Washington, it is lined with the nation’s most famous monuments and memorials, from the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial to the Vietnam Veterans and Martin Luther King Jr. memorials. It has also been the nation’s stage for inaugurations, celebrations, and protests, including the 1963 March on Washington.
location: Washington, D.C., from the U.S. Capitol to the Potomac River
thumbAlt: Aerial view of the National Mall

title: Route 66
subtitle: The “Mother Road” from Chicago to Santa Monica
summary: U.S. Highway 66 was created in 1926 to meet the growing demand for automobile travel. Its roughly 2,400 miles from Chicago to Santa Monica linked the main streets of small towns to cities, carried migrants fleeing the Dust Bowl and military convoys in World War II, and fed the boom in postwar road-trip tourism. Decommissioned in 1985, “Route 66” lives on in literature, film, and song as a symbol of mobility, freedom, and the American Dream.
location: Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California
thumbAlt: A Route 66 highway shield sign

title: St. Augustine
subtitle: The oldest continuously occupied European-founded city in the United States
summary: Spanish forces under Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine on September 8, 1565, at the site of a Timucua village called Seloy. Built to guard the route of Spain’s treasure fleets and to drive out a French Protestant colony nearby, it began a Spanish presence in Florida that lasted, with one interruption, for more than two centuries. It was founded decades before the English reached Jamestown.
thumbAlt: Aerial view of the Castillo de San Marcos and the town of St. Augustine, Florida, 1965

title: Statue of Liberty
subtitle: France’s gift to the United States, and a welcome to generations of immigrants
summary: The Statue of Liberty, officially Liberty Enlightening the World, was a gift from the people of France, designed by sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi with an iron framework by Gustave Eiffel, on a pedestal paid for by Americans. Dedicated on October 28, 1886, in New York Harbor, it was meant to celebrate American independence and French-American friendship. Next to Ellis Island, and later inscribed with Emma Lazarus’s poem “The New Colossus,” it became a symbol of welcome to immigrants.
thumbAlt: The Statue of Liberty on its pedestal, holding up her torch

title: The White House
subtitle: The president’s home and office since 1800, built partly by enslaved workers, burned in 1814 and rebuilt more than once
summary: The White House has been the home and workplace of every American president since John and Abigail Adams moved in, in November 1800. Designed by the Irish-born architect James Hoban, it was built between 1792 and 1800 by free workers and by enslaved people hired out by their owners. British troops burned it in 1814, and Hoban rebuilt it. Long called the “President’s House” or “Executive Mansion,” it got its official name from Theodore Roosevelt in 1901. Today it is a residence, an office, a stage for ceremonies, and a museum visited by hundreds of thousands of people a year.
thumbAlt: The north front of the White House, with its columned portico, seen across the lawn

title: Yellowstone National Park
subtitle: The world’s first national park, set aside in 1872 on top of an active volcano
summary: On March 1, 1872, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law that set aside more than two million acres of the Rocky Mountains, mostly in what is now Wyoming, as “a public park or pleasuring-ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people.” Yellowstone became the world’s first national park. It sits on one of the world’s largest volcanic calderas and holds more than half of all the geysers on Earth. People had lived in and traveled through the region for more than 11,000 years before it became a park.
thumbAlt: Thomas Moran’s 1872 painting of the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone, with the Lower Falls between golden cliffs

title: The American Revolution
subtitle: The war for independence from Britain, 1775–1783, and the revolution in ideas that made a new nation
summary: In little more than a decade after 1763, colonists who had been proud to be British came to see Parliament’s taxes and controls as a threat to their liberty, and in 1776 they declared independence. The war that followed, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord in April 1775 to the Treaty of Paris in September 1783, pitted the new United States, with France as its ally from 1778, against the world’s largest military. The Revolution created a republic founded on the idea that government rests on the consent of the governed, but it left slavery in place and opened Native lands to settlement, contradictions that shaped the nation for generations.
location: The thirteen colonies, the Atlantic, and battlefields from Canada to Georgia
thumbAlt: John Trumbull’s painting of the British surrender at Yorktown

title: The Civil War
subtitle: The war for union and against slavery, 1861–1865
summary: The Civil War was fought between the United States and eleven Southern states that seceded after Abraham Lincoln’s election in 1860 to form the Confederate States of America, a nation whose leaders openly identified it with slavery. It began with the Confederate bombardment of Fort Sumter in April 1861 and ended with Robert E. Lee’s surrender at Appomattox Court House in April 1865. What started as a war to preserve the Union became, through the actions of enslaved people, Congress, and Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation, a war to end slavery. It was the deadliest war in American history: traditional counts put the dead at about 620,000, and more recent estimates at about 750,000.
location: From Virginia and the Mississippi Valley to the border states, the Southwest, and the sea
thumbAlt: Currier and Ives print of the Battle of Gettysburg

title: The Cold War
subtitle: The global rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, 1947–1991
summary: The Cold War was a global political and ideological rivalry between the capitalist countries led by the United States and the communist countries led by the Soviet Union. It grew out of the failure of the World War II allies to agree on the postwar world and lasted from the late 1940s until the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991. The two superpowers never fought each other directly. Instead they built rival alliances, raced to build nuclear weapons and to reach space, and backed opposing sides in wars from Korea to Vietnam. The closest they came to nuclear war was the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962.
location: Worldwide: Europe, East Asia, Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa, the Middle East, and the arms and space races
thumbAlt: Map of Cold War alliances in 1974

title: The French and Indian War
subtitle: The North American front of the Seven Years’ War, 1754–1763
summary: The French and Indian War was a contest between Britain and France, and their colonists and Native allies, for control of eastern North America. It began in 1754 with a clash in the Ohio Valley involving a young George Washington and became part of a global war. Britain won, gaining Canada and the lands east of the Mississippi, but the debts and frontier conflicts it inherited set off the quarrels that led to the American Revolution.
location: Ohio Valley, New York, Pennsylvania, Canada, and the Great Lakes
thumbAlt: Illustration of George Washington on horseback at the Battle of the Monongahela

title: Persian Gulf War
subtitle: The U.S.-led coalition that expelled Iraq from Kuwait, 1990–1991
summary: On August 2, 1990, Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein invaded and annexed neighboring Kuwait. President George H. W. Bush organized a broad international coalition, backed by United Nations resolutions, and built up forces in Saudi Arabia (Operation Desert Shield). When Iraq refused to withdraw, the coalition launched an air war in January 1991 (Operation Desert Storm), followed by a ground offensive that drove Iraqi forces out of Kuwait in four days. The swift victory boosted Bush’s popularity and seemed to many to exorcise the “ghosts of Vietnam.”
thumbAlt: U.S. Air Force jets flying over burning Kuwaiti oil fields during Desert Storm

title: Iraq War
subtitle: The U.S. invasion and occupation of Iraq, 2003–2011
summary: In March 2003, the United States led an invasion of Iraq to overthrow Saddam Hussein, whom the Bush administration accused of possessing weapons of mass destruction and linked to terrorism. Baghdad fell within weeks, but no weapons of mass destruction were ever found, and a long, bloody insurgency followed. A 2007 troop “surge” reduced violence, and the last U.S. combat forces left in December 2011. The war remains one of the most controversial in American history.
thumbAlt: The toppling of Saddam Hussein’s statue in Baghdad

title: Korean War
subtitle: The first major armed conflict of the Cold War, 1950–1953
summary: On June 25, 1950, communist North Korea invaded South Korea. Under a United Nations mandate, the United States led a multinational force to defend the South. After dramatic swings (a near-collapse, the landing at Inchon, a drive to the Chinese border, and a massive Chinese intervention), the war settled into a bloody stalemate near the 38th parallel. An armistice in July 1953 ended the fighting but left Korea divided. More than 30,000 Americans and millions of Koreans died.
thumbAlt: U.S. Marines climbing a seawall during the Inchon landing

title: The Mexican-American War
subtitle: The United States conquers half of Mexico, 1846–1848
