summary: Within a year of annexing Texas, the United States went to war with Mexico over a disputed border and President James K. Polk’s ambition to acquire California and the Southwest. American armies occupied northern Mexico and California and captured Mexico City in September 1847. In the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Mexico ceded about 55 percent of its territory. The conquest fulfilled dreams of continental expansion, and immediately reopened the question of whether slavery would spread into the new lands.
location: Texas, northern Mexico, New Mexico, California, and central Mexico
thumbAlt: Carl Nebel’s print of General Winfield Scott’s entry into Mexico City

title: The Spanish-American War
subtitle: A short war that made the United States an overseas empire, 1898
summary: In 1898 the United States went to war with Spain over Cuba, where revolutionaries had been fighting for independence since 1895. In less than four months, U.S. forces destroyed Spanish fleets at Manila Bay and Santiago and defeated Spanish garrisons in Cuba. In the peace treaty, Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States, which also annexed Hawaii during the war. Victory made the United States a colonial power, and led directly to a bloody war against Filipino independence fighters.
location: Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, and Guam
thumbAlt: Theodore Roosevelt and the Rough Riders on San Juan Hill in 1898

title: The Vietnam War
subtitle: America’s longest war of the Cold War era, 1964–1973
summary: The Vietnam War was a long struggle over the future of Vietnam in which the United States fought to keep a non-communist South Vietnam from being reunited with the communist North. It grew out of Vietnam’s war for independence from France and the American belief that if one country fell to communism, its neighbors would follow. American involvement deepened from advisers in the 1950s to more than 500,000 troops by 1968. Unable to win, the United States withdrew under the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973, and in April 1975 North Vietnamese forces took Saigon and reunified the country. The war killed 58,220 Americans, divided American society, and shook Americans’ trust in their government.
thumbAlt: A U.S. soldier guiding a UH-1 helicopter in to land in Vietnam

title: War in Afghanistan
subtitle: America’s longest war, 2001–2021
summary: After the September 11 attacks, the United States invaded Afghanistan to destroy al-Qaeda and topple the Taliban government that sheltered it. Kabul fell within weeks, but Osama bin Laden escaped, and the Taliban regrouped. For twenty years American and NATO forces fought an insurgency while trying to build a stable Afghan government. U.S. forces killed bin Laden in Pakistan in 2011. When the last American troops withdrew hastily in August 2021, the Taliban immediately retook the country. It was the longest war in American history.
location: Afghanistan and the Pakistan border region
thumbAlt: U.S. soldiers on horseback in Afghanistan in 2001

title: The War of 1812
subtitle: The United States fights Britain again, 1812–1815
summary: Caught between Britain and France in the Napoleonic Wars, the United States declared war on Britain in 1812 over the seizure of American sailors and ships, and over western expansion and British support for Native resistance. American invasions of Canada failed; British troops burned Washington; and the 1814 Treaty of Ghent ended the war essentially as a draw. Yet Americans remembered it as a “second war of independence,” while for Native nations east of the Mississippi it was a decisive defeat.
location: Canada and the Great Lakes, the Chesapeake, the Gulf Coast, and the Atlantic
thumbAlt: Illustration of the British burning of Washington in 1814

title: World War I
subtitle: The United States enters the Great War, 1917–1918
summary: The United States stayed neutral for nearly three years after war broke out in Europe in 1914. Germany’s resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare and its secret proposal of an alliance with Mexico led President Woodrow Wilson to ask Congress for war in April 1917. More than two million American soldiers reached France, helping break Germany’s last offensives in 1918; more than 115,000 died, many from the influenza pandemic. At home, the war brought mobilization, propaganda, and repression of dissent. Wilson’s plans for a peace built on his Fourteen Points and a League of Nations foundered in the Senate.
location: Western Front in France and Belgium; the Atlantic; the home front
thumbAlt: James Montgomery Flagg’s “I Want You” recruiting poster

title: World War II
subtitle: The United States in the global war, 1941–1945
summary: World War II was the deadliest and most destructive war in human history: perhaps eighty million people died. The United States entered after Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, and fought alongside Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and other Allies against Germany, Italy, and Japan. The Soviet Union bore the heaviest burden of the war against Germany and broke Hitler’s army, while American factories armed the Allies and American forces fought in North Africa, Italy, and France and across the Pacific. The war ended with Germany’s surrender in May 1945 and Japan’s in August, after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It left the United States the world’s leading economic and military power.
location: Europe, North Africa, the Pacific and Asia, the Atlantic; the home front
thumbAlt: Japan’s foreign minister signing the instrument of surrender aboard USS Missouri
